evidence.snippet: Deposition of a well-organized collagen-based extracellular matrix network protects the heart from catastrophic rupture and attenuates ventricular dilation.
evidence.explanation: Evidences the protective role of organized collagen scar in limiting rupture and dilation.

evidence.snippet: Excessive, prolonged, or dysregulated inflammatory or fibrogenic cascades accentuate adverse remodeling and dysfunction.
evidence.explanation: Supports that dysregulated fibrogenic signaling drives adverse ventricular remodeling and dysfunction.

steps/4.description: Loss of contractile myocardium and sustained inflammatory/neurohormonal drive produce adverse structural remodeling of the ventricle. Cardiac fibroblasts differentiate into myofibroblasts that deposit a collagen-based extracellular matrix; a well-organized scar protects against rupture and limits acute dilation, but excessive, prolonged, or dysregulated fibrogenic signaling drives interstitial fibrosis, chamber dilation, and contractile dysfunction, progressing to heart failure. This node conforms to the conserved ventricular-remodeling step of the maladaptive-cardiomyopathy module, substituting the ischemic infarct scar as the disorder-specific insult.

steps/5.description: Chest pain is the cardinal presenting symptom of MI. This entry captures the broad symptom, including atypical or non-anginal chest pain and painless ("silent") presentations that are common in women, older adults, and people with diabetes; the classic ischemic substernal pain is captured separately as Angina pectoris.

steps/6.description: Ischemic necrosis of myocardium.

steps/7.description: Ischemia creates an arrhythmogenic substrate (e.g., ventricular arrhythmias).

steps/8.description: Loss of contractile myocardium reduces systolic function and can progress to heart failure.

steps/9.description: Prolonged substernal ischemic chest pressure/pain is the classic (typical) presenting symptom of acute MI, distinct from the atypical/non-anginal presentations captured under Chest pain.

steps/10.description: Shortness of breath, a common presenting symptom and a feature of MI-related heart failure.

steps/11.description: Malignant ventricular arrhythmia that can complicate acute ischemia/reperfusion and cause sudden cardiac death.

steps/12.description: Adverse ventricular remodeling after infarction can progress to heart failure.

steps/13.description: Transient loss of consciousness may occur, e.g., from arrhythmia or hemodynamic compromise.

edges/0.description: Occlusive coronary thrombosis abruptly interrupts perfusion of the downstream myocardium, producing ischemia.

edges/1.description: Emergency restoration of coronary flow to salvage ischemic myocardium paradoxically inflicts additional reperfusion injury on the jeopardized tissue.

edges/2.description: Massive cardiomyocyte death releases damage-associated molecular patterns that ignite the post-infarction inflammatory and reparative cascade.

edges/3.description: Regional ischemic necrosis of myocardium is the infarct itself, so this node is what the clinical phenotype names.

edges/4.description: Ischemic myocardium generates the prolonged substernal pressure or pain of the classic acute presentation, transmitted by cardiac sympathetic afferents.

edges/5.description: The same ischemic afferent signalling also produces atypical and non-anginal chest discomfort, which is how a large fraction of infarcts present.

edges/6.description: Ischemic and necrotic myocardium is electrically heterogeneous and provides the arrhythmogenic substrate for conduction block and re-entry.

edges/7.description: Loss of contractile myocardium in the infarct territory reduces global left ventricular systolic performance.

edges/8.description: Abrupt restoration of flow into ischemic myocardium produces calcium overload and marked dispersion of repolarization at the border zone, the substrate for reperfusion ventricular fibrillation.

edges/9.description: Reperfusion-driven necrosis and DAMP release amplify the sterile inflammatory response in the infarcted myocardium.

edges/10.description: Efferocytosis-driven release of TGF-beta and other reparative mediators activates fibroblasts and myofibroblasts, initiating fibrotic scar formation and structural remodeling.

edges/11.description: Interstitial fibrosis and chamber dilation degrade contractile efficiency beyond the initial loss of infarcted muscle, lowering ejection fraction further in the months after the event.

edges/12.description: Adverse post-infarction remodeling progresses to the congestive heart-failure syndrome once systolic dysfunction and neurohormonal activation raise filling pressures and cause fluid retention.

edges/13.description: Ventricular ectopy arising on the ischemic substrate can degenerate into ventricular fibrillation, the malignant end of the post-infarction arrhythmia spectrum.

edges/14.description: A sustained brady- or tachyarrhythmia drops cardiac output abruptly enough to cause transient cerebral hypoperfusion and loss of consciousness.

edges/15.description: Impaired systolic emptying raises filling pressures and congests the pulmonary circulation, which is felt as breathlessness.

evidence.snippet: implementation of care delivery systems prioritising immediate revascularisation through percutaneous coronary intervention (or fibrinolysis)
evidence.explanation: Identifies immediate revascularisation by PCI or fibrinolysis as central to modern AMI management.

treatments/0.description: Emergency restoration of coronary blood flow by primary percutaneous coronary intervention or, where unavailable, fibrinolysis, to salvage ischemic myocardium.

evidence.snippet: implementation of care delivery systems prioritising immediate revascularisation through percutaneous coronary intervention (or fibrinolysis)
evidence.explanation: Identifies immediate revascularisation by PCI or fibrinolysis as central to modern AMI management.

treatments/0/targets/0.description: Primary PCI or fibrinolysis removes or lyses the occlusive coronary thrombus and restores antegrade flow in the infarct-related artery.

treatments/0/targets/1.description: Restoring perfusion salvages myocardium that has not yet infarcted, which is the point of treating within a time window; the same manoeuvre also opens the reperfusion-injury node modelled downstream.

evidence.snippet: advances in antiplatelet agents and anticoagulants, and greater use of secondary prevention strategies such as statins.
evidence.explanation: Identifies antiplatelet agents, anticoagulants, and statins as pillars of pharmacological AMI management.

treatments/1.description: Antiplatelet agents and anticoagulants to limit coronary thrombus propagation, plus secondary-prevention statins.

evidence.snippet: advances in antiplatelet agents and anticoagulants, and greater use of secondary prevention strategies such as statins.
evidence.explanation: Identifies antiplatelet agents, anticoagulants, and statins as pillars of pharmacological AMI management.

treatments/1/targets/0.description: Antiplatelet agents and anticoagulants limit propagation of thrombus on the disrupted plaque and reduce re-occlusion after reperfusion; the secondary-prevention statin component acts on the underlying atheroma.

evidence.snippet: including IL-1 and IL-6 inhibitors such as Canakinumab and Tocilizumab
evidence.explanation: Identifies IL-1 (canakinumab) and IL-6 (tocilizumab) inhibitors as immunotherapeutic strategies in MI/MIRI.

treatments/2.description: Emerging cytokine-directed therapy targeting the post-infarction inflammatory response, notably IL-1 (canakinumab) and IL-6 (tocilizumab) pathway inhibitors, to reduce cardiovascular events and mitigate ischemia-reperfusion injury.

evidence.snippet: including IL-1 and IL-6 inhibitors such as Canakinumab and Tocilizumab
evidence.explanation: Identifies IL-1 (canakinumab) and IL-6 (tocilizumab) inhibitors as immunotherapeutic strategies in MI/MIRI.

treatments/2/targets/0.description: IL-1 and IL-6 pathway blockade damps the cytokine arm of the post-infarction inflammatory response. The effect is deliberately recorded as modulation rather than inhibition, since this response is required for healing and only its excessive form is adverse.

treatments/2/targets/1.description: The same cytokine-directed agents are under study to mitigate ischemia-reperfusion injury, in which NLRP3 inflammasome and IL-1 signalling are prominent.

evidence.snippet: Myotonic Dystrophy type 1 (DM1) is a neuromuscular disease showing strong genetic anticipation, and is caused by the expansion of a CTG repeat tract in the 3'-UTR of the DMPK gene.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the causal repeat expansion and anticipation.

evidence.snippet: In 1992, the mutation responsible for DM1 was identified as a CTG expansion located in the 3' untranslated region of the dystrophia myotonica-protein kinase gene (DMPK).
evidence.explanation: Review-level evidence confirms the initiating DMPK 3'-UTR CTG expansion.

steps/1.description: DM1 begins with an unstable CTG trinucleotide repeat expansion in the 3'-untranslated region of DMPK. The repeat-expansion allele is germline, autosomal dominant, and becomes more unstable across generations and across tissues, providing the initiating mutation for downstream RNA toxicity.

evidence.snippet: Introducing the (CTG)84 allele into an Msh3-deficient background completely blocked the somatic repeat instability.
evidence.explanation: DM1 knock-in mice show that Msh3 (the MutSβ partner) is required for all somatic CTG expansion — the CTG-class instance of the module's aberrant-MMR mechanism.

evidence.snippet: higher FAN1 expression was associated with reduced somatic expansion and later onset.
evidence.explanation: In DM1 patients the DNA-repair modifier FAN1 is protective — higher expression means less somatic expansion and later onset — mirroring the module's FAN1-protective arm and the somatic-expansion→onset link.

steps/2.description: Beyond the inherited germline expansion, the DMPK CTG repeat continues to expand somatically throughout life, driven by aberrant DNA mismatch repair (the MutSβ/MSH3 complex licenses expansion; FAN1 is protective). Somatic expansion is progressive with age and tissue-specific — largest in the most clinically affected tissues such as skeletal muscle — and its rate, set by the expression balance of DNA-repair modifiers, tracks disease severity and age of onset. This ongoing somatic expansion continually raises the expanded-CUG RNA burden that drives the downstream RNA-toxicity cascade.

evidence.snippet: In both types of myotonic dystrophy the expanded repeat is transcribed and the RNA produced from the mutant allele is retained in nuclear inclusions. Recent studies suggest that the mutant RNA has a toxic effect on muscle fibers by interfering with the essential functions of the myonucleus, such as RNA processing.
evidence.explanation: Confirms the toxic RNA gain-of-function mechanism in myotonic dystrophy.

evidence.snippet: the clinical features common to both diseases are caused by a gain-of-function RNA mechanism in which the CUG and CCUG repeats alter cellular function, including alternative splicing of various genes.
evidence.explanation: Supports the toxic RNA gain-of-function mechanism and its connection to altered splicing.

evidence.snippet: Altogether, these observations argue that the persistence of nuclear-retained CUG RNAs, independent of higher-order RNA assemblies, titrates MBNL1 and contributes to disease progression.
evidence.explanation: Quantitative imaging in a patient-derived myotube model relocates the toxic species from the visible focus to the individual nuclear-retained transcript, which is why this node is framed around nuclear retention rather than focus formation.

steps/3.description: The expanded DMPK repeat is transcribed into CUG repeat-containing RNA that is retained in the nucleus and recruits RNA-binding proteins that normally regulate adult splicing programs. Nuclear retention, rather than the higher-order focus itself, is the toxic state: quantitative imaging in patient-derived myotubes shows that most objects scored as "foci" are single RNA molecules, and that these individual nuclear-retained transcripts titrate MBNL1. Multimeric foci arise from transcriptional bursting, dissociate over time, and depend on MBNL proteins for their own assembly, so they are better read as a marker of the retained-RNA burden than as the pathogenic species.

evidence.snippet: Mutant RNA sequesters MBNL1, a splice regulator protein and depletes MBNL1 from the nucleoplasm. Loss of MBNL1 results in altered splicing of ClC-1 mRNA.
evidence.explanation: Describes the MBNL1 depletion mechanism that drives DM1 spliceopathy.

evidence.snippet: The pathogenesis of DM involves a RNA gain-of-function mechanism caused by expression of mutant RNAs containing hundred to thousands of CUG or CCUG repeats that interfere with the splicing of other pre-mRNAs through dysfunction of two classes of RNA-binding proteins.
evidence.explanation: Supports the broader spliceopathy mechanism downstream of expanded repeat RNA.

evidence.snippet: We found that the majority of changes induced by CUG(exp) RNA in skeletal muscle can be explained by reduced activity of Mbnl1, including many changes that are secondary to myotonia.
evidence.explanation: Transcriptome-wide comparison of CUG-expansion transgenic, Mbnl1 knockout, and Clcn1 null mice quantifies how much of the DM1 expression signature the MBNL1 arm accounts for. The same study qualifies the node: the effects are mediated mainly but not entirely through Mbnl1, with transcription and mRNA decay also contributing.

evidence.snippet: Activation of PKC is required for CUGBP1 hyperphosphorylation in DM1 cells, and PKCalpha and betaII directly phosphorylate CUGBP1 in vitro.
evidence.explanation: Supplies the mechanism for the CELF1/CUGBP1 arm this node asserts: CUG-repeat RNA expression raises steady-state CUGBP1 by PKC-mediated hyperphosphorylation and protein stabilization, not by transcriptional induction.

evidence.snippet: In contrast, CELF1 was elevated in nuclei of mature myofibers of the DM1 model, consistent with a primary effect of pathogenic RNA expression.
evidence.explanation: Distinguishes the DM1 CELF1 elevation from the DM1-like splicing changes that also appear in four non-DM1 dystrophy models and two myotoxin injury models. There the changes track regenerating fibers; only in the DM1 model is CELF1 raised in mature myofibers, which is what makes it a primary consequence of the toxic RNA rather than a regeneration artifact.

steps/4.description: Expanded CUG RNA sequesters MBNL family proteins in nuclear foci and is accompanied by increased CELF1/CUGBP1 activity in affected tissues. The resulting loss of adult MBNL activity and CELF1/MBNL imbalance causes fetal-pattern alternative splicing across skeletal muscle, heart, endocrine, and CNS transcripts.

evidence.snippet: Altered splice products do not encode functional ClC-1 protein. Subsequent loss of chloride conductance in muscle membrane causes myotonia in the myotonic dystrophies.
evidence.explanation: Directly links CLCN1 mis-splicing to reduced chloride conductance and myotonia.

steps/5.description: MBNL1 sequestration causes mis-splicing of the chloride channel gene CLCN1, leading to loss of functional ClC-1 chloride channels in skeletal muscle membranes. Reduced chloride conductance causes membrane hyperexcitability and myotonia.

evidence.snippet: The extent of E29 skipping correlated with severity of weakness in tibialis anterior muscle of DM1 patients.
evidence.explanation: Human muscle data link CACNA1S exon 29 skipping to weakness severity.

steps/6.description: DM1 spliceopathy represses inclusion of CACNA1S/CaV1.1 exon 29 in skeletal muscle. CaV1.1 controls excitation-contraction coupling, so this splice shift changes calcium-channel gating and contributes to progressive muscle weakness and myopathic changes.

evidence.snippet: alternative splicing of the insulin receptor (IR) pre-mRNA is aberrantly regulated in DM1 skeletal muscle tissue, resulting in predominant expression of the lower-signaling nonmuscle isoform (IR-A).
evidence.explanation: Directly supports the INSR splice shift that produces an insulin-resistant skeletal muscle phenotype.

steps/7.description: Aberrant splicing of insulin receptor pre-mRNA in DM1 skeletal muscle favors the lower-signaling IR-A isoform, reducing metabolic insulin responsiveness and contributing to insulin resistance and diabetes mellitus.

evidence.snippet: Using RNA sequencing, here we identify novel splicing alterations in DM heart samples, including a switch from adult exon 6B towards fetal exon 6A in the cardiac sodium channel, SCN5A.
evidence.explanation: Human heart RNA-seq identifies the SCN5A splice shift.

evidence.snippet: We showed that correction Scn5a mis-splicing does not improve the DM1 heart conduction delays and structural changes induced by CUG repeat RNA expression.
evidence.explanation: Refutes the sufficiency of this branch, not its existence. Mice engineered to lack Scn5a exon 6A, and so locked onto the adult exon 6B isoform, were crossed into the CUG960 DM1 heart model and showed no improvement in conduction delay or structural change. The splice shift is real and contributes, but correcting it alone rescues nothing.

steps/8.description: In DM1 heart tissue, MBNL-dependent spliceopathy shifts SCN5A from the adult exon 6B isoform toward the fetal exon 6A isoform. The resulting Nav1.5 channel has reduced excitability, providing a mutation-to-cardiac conduction defect branch in the pathograph. This branch contributes but is not sufficient: forcing the adult exon 6B isoform in a CUG960 DM1 heart model leaves conduction delay and structural change unimproved, so DM1 cardiac disease is not the sum of this splicing defect. See the Splicing-Independent Progressive Cardiac Pathology node for the parallel arm, and the dm1_nonsplicing_cardiac_progression discussion for what remains unresolved.

evidence.snippet: BIN1 missplicing results in expression of an inactive form of BIN1 lacking phosphatidylinositol 5-phosphate-binding and membrane-tubulating activities.
evidence.explanation: Fugier et al. Nat Med 2011 directly demonstrated BIN1 mis-splicing in DM1 patient muscle, with loss of membrane-tubulation activity. T-tubule alterations and muscle weakness were reproduced in mice by recapitulating the BIN1 splicing shift.

steps/9.description: MBNL1 sequestration in DM1 causes mis-splicing of bridging integrator-1 (BIN1) pre-mRNA in skeletal muscle, producing an inactive BIN1 isoform lacking phosphatidylinositol 5-phosphate-binding and membrane-tubulating activities. T-tubule biogenesis is impaired, disrupting excitation-contraction coupling and contributing to the muscle weakness that is distinct from myotonia (driven by CLCN1).

evidence.snippet: This leads to the sequestration of splicing factors such as muscleblind-like 1/2 (MBNL1/2) and aberrant splicing in the central nervous system.
evidence.explanation: Human brain study supports CNS MBNL sequestration and aberrant splicing.

evidence.snippet: Myotonic dystrophy type 1 (DM1) is an inherited autosomal-dominant condition that induces altered splicing of transcripts, including MAPT, leading to a distinctive abnormal deposition of tau protein in the CNS.
evidence.explanation: Human neuropathology links MAPT spliceopathy and CNS tau deposition.

steps/10.description: DM1 affects the central nervous system through MBNL1/2 sequestration and aberrant brain splicing. MAPT/tau transcript dysregulation and abnormal tau deposition provide a mechanistic bridge to cognitive and behavioral impairment.

evidence.snippet: We demonstrate that an abnormal accumulation of p16 is responsible for this defect because the abolition of p16 activity overcomes early growth arrest and restores an extended proliferative capacity.
evidence.explanation: The p16 removal experiment is what makes this causal rather than correlative in cultured DM1 muscle precursor cells. The upstream link from the expanded repeat to p16 accumulation is described only as a cellular stress and remains uncharacterized, and the connection to muscle wasting in vivo is proposed rather than shown.

steps/11.description: DM1 muscle precursor cells carrying large CTG expansions stop dividing early not because they have used up their replicative capacity but because they enter premature senescence. p16 accumulates abnormally, and abolishing p16 activity overcomes the early growth arrest and restores extended proliferation; accelerated telomere shortening, which is also present, does not account for the p16 induction. Because the reserve is arrested rather than exhausted, this is a candidate contributor to impaired regeneration and atrophy in large-expansion DM1 that is separable from the spliceopathy.

evidence.snippet: respiratory dysfunction, predominantly a restrictive ventilatory pattern, is common in myotonic dystrophy and is associated with alveolar hypoventilation, chronic hypercapnia, and sleep disturbance in the form of sleep apnoea and sleep related disordered breathing;
evidence.explanation: Systematic review supports respiratory dysfunction and its major physiologic components in DM1.

steps/12.description: Respiratory morbidity in DM1 reflects both peripheral respiratory muscle weakness and central respiratory drive involvement. The result is commonly restrictive ventilatory dysfunction with alveolar hypoventilation, chronic hypercapnia, and sleep-disordered breathing.

evidence.snippet: Sustained CUGexp RNA expression caused progressive cardiac enlargement, contractile dysfunction, conduction delay, myocardial fibrosis, and reduced survival, while MBNL-dependent splicing defects remained static, consistent with the stable repeat length.
evidence.explanation: Dissociates cardiac progression from both spliceopathy severity and somatic repeat expansion, since repeat length is fixed by the transgene and the splicing readouts do not move while the phenotype worsens.

evidence.snippet: Suppression of CUGexp RNA expression rescued cardiac abnormalities, but reversibility declined with longer exposure to the toxic RNA.
evidence.explanation: Establishes that the branch is driven by ongoing CUG RNA expression and is reversible early, while the loss of reversibility with duration is what marks it as progressive rather than a steady-state deficit.

evidence.snippet: We showed that correction Scn5a mis-splicing does not improve the DM1 heart conduction delays and structural changes induced by CUG repeat RNA expression.
evidence.explanation: The complementary argument for this node: the best-characterized cardiac splicing defect can be fully corrected without benefit, so a splicing-independent arm is required to account for the phenotype.

steps/13.description: Cardiac disease in DM1 worsens over time through a route that does not run through the MBNL-dependent spliceopathy. In an inducible heart-specific model expressing a stable, interrupted 960-CUG-repeat RNA — a design that holds repeat length fixed and so excludes somatic expansion — sustained expression produced progressive cardiac enlargement, contractile dysfunction, conduction delay, myocardial fibrosis, and reduced survival while MBNL-dependent splicing defects stayed static. Suppressing the transgene rescued the cardiac abnormalities, but reversibility fell with longer exposure, implying a component that accumulates rather than simply tracking the current RNA burden. The intermediate steps between persistent nuclear CUG RNA and fibrotic and contractile failure are not identified.

evidence.snippet: The upregulated genes in DM1 and DM2 were highly enriched in both interferon-regulated genes (IRGs) and genes associated with the response to dsRNA and the innate immune response.
evidence.explanation: Array profiling of human DM1 and DM2 cataract lens samples against non-DM cataract controls. The DM1/DM2 overlap is what argues for a repeat-RNA mechanism shared by two different genes rather than a DMPK locus effect, which is the respect in which it is independent of the SIX5 branch.

steps/14.description: Transcription of the expanded repeat produces double-stranded RNA in DM cells, and lens tissue from DM1 and DM2 cataracts carries a shared transcriptional signature dominated by interferon-regulated genes and dsRNA-response genes, with 83 percent of dysregulated genes common to the two diseases. This is a candidate lens mechanism sitting outside the MBNL1/CELF1 splicing axis. It is an expression association in surgical specimens: no perturbation was performed, there is no MBNL1 comparison arm, and the signature has not been shown to precede or cause opacity, so its weight relative to the SIX5 locus branch is unresolved.

evidence.snippet: Our results demonstrate that the rate and severity of cataract formation is inversely related to Six5 dosage and is temporally progressive.
evidence.explanation: Six5 dosage model supports a cataract mechanism connected to the DMPK/SIX5 locus.

evidence.snippet: real-time PCR analysis showed reduced SIX5 expression and increased expression of the Ca(2+)-activated K(+) channel SK3 in the DM1 cells
evidence.explanation: Human counterpart to the mouse Six5 dosage data. Lens epithelial cell lines derived from DM1 cataracts carry large repeat expansions, reduced SIX5, and raised SK3, and both the excess calcium-stimulated potassium efflux and the excess cell death are blocked by the SK inhibitor apamin. SIX5 reduction is measured rather than manipulated here, so the SIX5-to-opacity step remains inferred.

steps/15.description: The DM1 CTG repeat lies near SIX5, and repeat-associated local chromatin or transcriptional effects can reduce SIX5 dosage. Mouse Six5 loss produces progressive ocular cataracts, supporting a parallel lens branch in addition to toxic RNA spliceopathy.

evidence.snippet: Myotonia reflects a state of muscle fiber hyperexcitability. Impaired transmembrane conductance of either chloride or sodium ions results in myotonia.
evidence.explanation: Confirms myotonia as the defining feature resulting from ion channel dysfunction.

evidence.snippet: HP:0003740 | Myotonia with warm-up phenomenon | Very frequent (99-80%)
evidence.explanation: Orphanet records myotonia with warm-up phenomenon as a very frequent HPO phenotype for Steinert myotonic dystrophy / DM1.

steps/16.description: Myotonia, the hallmark symptom, is characterized by delayed relaxation of skeletal muscle after contraction. Patients describe stiffness that improves with repeated muscle contractions (warm-up phenomenon).

evidence.snippet: The extent of E29 skipping correlated with severity of weakness in tibialis anterior muscle of DM1 patients.
evidence.explanation: Provides a direct molecular correlation between CaV1.1 mis-splicing and weakness severity.

evidence.snippet: HP:0002460 | Distal muscle weakness | Very frequent (99-80%)
evidence.explanation: Orphanet records distal muscle weakness as a very frequent HPO phenotype, matching the distal-predominant weakness described here.

steps/17.description: Progressive skeletal muscle weakness and wasting, particularly affecting distal muscles initially (grip, ankle dorsiflexors), with later involvement of proximal muscles and facial muscles.

evidence.snippet: Muscle weakness (92.2%), myotonia (85.9%), and fatigue (73.4%) were the most prevalent clinical features.
evidence.explanation: Directly documents fatigue as the third most prevalent DM1 clinical feature in a 64-patient genetically confirmed cohort.

evidence.snippet: HP:0012378 | Fatigue | Frequent (79-30%)
evidence.explanation: Orphanet records fatigue as a frequent HPO phenotype for Steinert myotonic dystrophy / DM1.

steps/18.description: Fatigue is among the most common complaints in DM1, affecting the majority of patients and substantially impairing quality of life and daily activity.

evidence.snippet: Perhaps the most noteworthy of these is the distinctive myotonic cataract which often appears early on in the course of the disorder.
evidence.explanation: Supports cataract as an early and characteristic ocular manifestation of myotonic dystrophy.

evidence.snippet: HP:0007787 | Posterior subcapsular cataract | Very frequent (99-80%)
evidence.explanation: Orphanet records posterior subcapsular cataract as a very frequent HPO phenotype for Steinert myotonic dystrophy / DM1.

steps/19.description: Posterior subcapsular cataracts are a characteristic finding, often present before age 50. Iridescent multicolored opacities (Christmas tree cataracts) are pathognomonic for DM1.

evidence.snippet: Cardiac alterations, characterized by conduction delays and arrhythmia, are the second most common cause of death in DM.
evidence.explanation: Supports conduction delay and arrhythmia as major cardiac manifestations of myotonic dystrophy.

evidence.snippet: HP:0031546 | Cardiac conduction abnormality | Very frequent (99-80%)
evidence.explanation: Orphanet records cardiac conduction abnormality as a very frequent HPO phenotype for Steinert myotonic dystrophy / DM1.

steps/20.description: Cardiac involvement includes conduction abnormalities (first-degree AV block, bundle branch block), arrhythmias, and cardiomyopathy. Cardiac complications are a leading cause of death in DM1.

evidence.snippet: People with DM1 have an unusual form of insulin resistance caused by a defect in skeletal muscle.
evidence.explanation: Supports the insulin resistance branch that contributes to the diabetes phenotype in DM1.

evidence.snippet: HP:0000819 | Diabetes mellitus | Occasional (29-5%)
evidence.explanation: Orphanet records diabetes mellitus as an occasional HPO phenotype for Steinert myotonic dystrophy / DM1.

steps/21.description: Endocrine manifestations include insulin resistance, diabetes mellitus, hypogonadism in males, and thyroid dysfunction.

evidence.snippet: Regarding the comorbidities, 4.7% of patients had tumors, 17.2% had diabetes, 23.4% had dyspnea, 28.1% had intermittent insomnia, 43.8% experienced dysphagia, and 25% exhibited cognitive impairment.
evidence.explanation: Directly documents cognitive impairment as a clinical manifestation in a genetically confirmed DM1 cohort.

evidence.snippet: HP:0100543 | Cognitive impairment | Frequent (79-30%)
evidence.explanation: Orphanet records cognitive impairment as a frequent HPO phenotype for Steinert myotonic dystrophy / DM1.

steps/22.description: Central nervous system involvement includes cognitive impairment, apathy, and other behavioral manifestations in adult DM1.

evidence.snippet: Of them, 70.3% of patients had daytime sleepiness, 14.1% had cataract surgery, 7.8% used wheelchairs, 4.7% required ventilatory support, and 1.6% required gastric tubes.
evidence.explanation: Directly supports excessive daytime somnolence as a very frequent DM1 phenotype.

evidence.snippet: HP:0001262 | Excessive daytime somnolence | Very frequent (99-80%)
evidence.explanation: Orphanet records excessive daytime somnolence as a very frequent HPO phenotype for Steinert myotonic dystrophy / DM1.

steps/23.description: Excessive daytime sleepiness is common in DM1 and can substantially affect daily functioning.

evidence.snippet: Regarding the comorbidities, 4.7% of patients had tumors, 17.2% had diabetes, 23.4% had dyspnea, 28.1% had intermittent insomnia, 43.8% experienced dysphagia, and 25% exhibited cognitive impairment.
evidence.explanation: Documents intermittent insomnia at 28.1% prevalence in a genetically confirmed DM1 cohort.

steps/24.description: Intermittent insomnia has been documented in DM1, contributing to overall sleep disturbance alongside excessive daytime somnolence.

evidence.snippet: Regarding the comorbidities, 4.7% of patients had tumors, 17.2% had diabetes, 23.4% had dyspnea, 28.1% had intermittent insomnia, 43.8% experienced dysphagia, and 25% exhibited cognitive impairment.
evidence.explanation: Directly supports dysphagia as a frequent clinical manifestation in DM1.

steps/25.description: Swallowing difficulty is a frequent multisystem manifestation of DM1 and can require nutritional support in advanced cases.

evidence.snippet: respiratory dysfunction, predominantly a restrictive ventilatory pattern, is common in myotonic dystrophy and is associated with alveolar hypoventilation, chronic hypercapnia, and sleep disturbance in the form of sleep apnoea and sleep related disordered breathing;
evidence.explanation: Supports respiratory insufficiency as a common respiratory manifestation with restrictive and hypoventilation physiology.

evidence.snippet: HP:0002093 | Respiratory insufficiency | Occasional (29-5%)
evidence.explanation: Orphanet records respiratory insufficiency as an occasional HPO phenotype for Steinert myotonic dystrophy / DM1.

steps/26.description: Respiratory failure from weakness of the diaphragm and intercostal muscles is a major cause of morbidity and mortality.

edges/2.description: The germline expanded allele is further expanded somatically across the lifespan and across tissues by aberrant mismatch repair.

edges/3.description: The expanded DMPK allele is transcribed into CUG repeat-containing RNA that accumulates in nuclear foci.

edges/4.description: The repeat expansion sits adjacent to SIX5, supporting a parallel locus-dosage branch for cataract susceptibility.

edges/5.description: Ongoing somatic CTG expansion increases the expanded-CUG RNA burden that accumulates in nuclear foci, intensifying the RNA-toxicity cascade.

edges/6.description: Nuclear-retained CUG RNA titrates MBNL proteins and shifts the CELF1/MBNL balance, producing widespread developmental splice reversion.

edges/7.description: Sustained expression of a repeat-length-stable CUG RNA drives progressive cardiac disease while MBNL-dependent splicing stays static, so at least one intermediate on this branch is not the spliceopathy and is not yet identified.

edges/8.description: Large CTG expansions push DM1 muscle precursor cells into p16-dependent premature senescence rather than replicative exhaustion.

edges/9.description: Repeat-containing transcripts accumulate as double-stranded RNA in DM cells and DM1 and DM2 lens tissue carries an interferon and dsRNA-response signature, but the sensor and the path to opacity are not established.

edges/10.description: MBNL1 depletion causes CLCN1 mis-splicing, loss of functional ClC-1 chloride channel, and skeletal muscle hyperexcitability.

edges/11.description: Mis-splicing of CaV1.1/CACNA1S alters excitation-contraction coupling in skeletal muscle and contributes to weakness.

edges/12.description: Oropharyngeal skeletal muscle spliceopathy contributes to swallowing dysfunction in DM1.

edges/13.description: Aberrant insulin receptor splicing favors the lower-signaling IR-A isoform in skeletal muscle.

edges/14.description: Cardiac spliceopathy shifts SCN5A toward a fetal exon 6A isoform with reduced excitability.

edges/15.description: MBNL1 sequestration drives BIN1 exon 11 mis-splicing, producing an inactive BIN1 isoform that disrupts T-tubule biogenesis and excitation-contraction coupling.

edges/16.description: MBNL1/2 sequestration in the CNS alters brain splicing programs, including MAPT/tau-related transcripts.

edges/17.description: Loss of functional ClC-1 chloride conductance causes the muscle hyperexcitability phenotype.

edges/18.description: Altered CaV1.1 gating impairs excitation-contraction coupling and contributes to progressive skeletal muscle weakness.

edges/19.description: Excitation-contraction coupling defects and myopathic changes can contribute to fatigue in DM1.

edges/20.description: The same skeletal muscle weakness branch can involve respiratory muscles and worsen ventilatory capacity.

edges/21.description: Predominant IR-A expression lowers insulin signaling in skeletal muscle and contributes to glucose intolerance and diabetes.

edges/22.description: Reduced excitability of the fetal SCN5A/Nav1.5 isoform contributes to conduction delay and arrhythmia, but is not sufficient for the DM1 cardiac phenotype: forcing the adult isoform in a DM1 heart model does not correct conduction delay or structural change.

edges/23.description: BIN1-driven T-tubule disruption impairs excitation-contraction coupling and contributes to progressive DM1 muscle weakness.

edges/24.description: CNS spliceopathy and tau dysregulation provide a mechanistic basis for cognitive impairment in DM1.

edges/25.description: CNS MBNL sequestration and aberrant brain splicing contribute to hypersomnia in DM1.

edges/26.description: CNS MBNL sequestration and disrupted sleep-wake circuitry contribute to sleep fragmentation and insomnia in DM1.

edges/27.description: DMPK/SIX5 locus effects provide a mutation-to-lens opacity path.

edges/28.description: Progressive structural remodeling and myocardial fibrosis accompany conduction delay in this model; the intermediate steps from persistent CUG RNA to remodeling are unidentified.

edges/29.description: Premature senescence of the muscle precursor pool is a candidate contributor to the progressive wasting and atrophy of large-expansion DM1.

edges/30.description: A candidate parallel route to lens opacity that does not depend on MBNL1 sequestration or on SIX5 dosage.

edges/31.description: Restrictive ventilatory impairment and hypoventilation manifest clinically as respiratory insufficiency.

evidence.snippet: Myotonic Dystrophy type 1 (DM1) is a neuromuscular disease showing strong genetic anticipation, and is caused by the expansion of a CTG repeat tract in the 3'-UTR of the DMPK gene.
evidence.explanation: Confirms the CTG expansion in DMPK as the causative mutation with genetic anticipation.

genes/0.notes: Expansion of CTG repeats in the 3'-UTR of DMPK on chromosome 19q13.3. Normal alleles have 5-34 repeats; affected individuals have 50 to >1000 repeats. Congenital DM1 is associated with very large expansions (>1000 repeats). Genetic anticipation occurs, with repeat length increasing across generations.

evidence.snippet: Cholesterol-lowering medications (i.e., statins), which can cause muscle pain and weakness; the anesthetic agent vecuronium; succinylcholine, propofol, and doxorubicin
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews lists these agents among those to avoid in DM1; statins can cause muscle pain/weakness and the anesthetic agents carry perioperative risk.

treatments/0.description: Several agents are contraindicated or hazardous in DM1 and should be avoided or used with caution, particularly perioperatively, given the risk of muscle, cardiac, and respiratory complications.

treatments/1.description: Mexiletine is the most commonly used antimyotonia agent. Other options include phenytoin and carbamazepine for symptomatic relief of myotonia.

evidence.snippet: Mexiletine at dosages of 150 and 200 mg 3 times daily is effective, safe, and well-tolerated over 7 weeks as an antimyotonia treatment in DM1.
evidence.explanation: Randomized crossover trials support mexiletine as symptomatic treatment for DM1 myotonia.

treatments/1/targets/0.description: Mexiletine is symptomatic antimyotonia pharmacotherapy that reduces delayed relaxation downstream of the CLCN1/chloride-conductance myotonia branch.

treatments/2.description: Regular cardiac monitoring with ECG and Holter is essential. Pacemaker or implantable cardioverter-defibrillator may be required for conduction defects or arrhythmias.

treatments/3.description: Multidisciplinary care including physical therapy, speech therapy, respiratory support (non-invasive ventilation), and ophthalmologic surveillance.

treatments/4.description: Genetic counseling is essential given autosomal dominant inheritance with anticipation. Congenital DM1 is almost exclusively maternally transmitted.

evidence.snippet: Baliforsen was generally well tolerated. However, skeletal muscle drug concentrations were below levels predicted to achieve substantial target reduction.
evidence.explanation: The trial's own interpretation, and the reason this entry is worded as tolerability without target engagement. Reaching predicted target reduction was the pharmacodynamic precondition for testing the mechanism, and it was not met.

treatments/5.description: Baliforsen (ISIS 598769) is an antisense oligonucleotide directed at DMPK mRNA, intended to lower the toxic CUG-repeat transcript at its source rather than treat a downstream symptom. It is investigational, not approved. In the completed multicentre, randomised, placebo-controlled phase 1/2a dose-escalation trial (NCT02312011, 48 dosed adults across five dose levels) it was generally well tolerated, with injection-site reactions, headache, contusion, and nausea the common adverse events and one case of transient thrombocytopenia. Muscle drug concentration rose with dose but stayed below the level predicted to achieve substantial target reduction, so this trial established tolerability and exposure without demonstrating target engagement. It should therefore not be cited as therapeutic corroboration of the RNA-toxicity mechanism; delivery to muscle is the limiting problem.

evidence.snippet: These results support the further investigation of ASOs as a therapeutic approach for myotonic dystrophy type 1, but suggest improved drug delivery to muscle is needed.
evidence.explanation: Supports the target rationale while marking the link as unproven in humans: the trialists conclude the approach is worth pursuing and that muscle delivery, not target choice, is what needs to improve.

treatments/5/targets/0.description: The ASO is designed to recruit RNase H1 to DMPK transcripts and reduce the nuclear-retained CUG-repeat RNA burden that titrates MBNL1. Whether the dosing achieved in this trial reduced that burden in muscle was not established.

evidence.snippet: Myotonic Dystrophy type 1 (DM1) is a neuromuscular disease showing strong genetic anticipation, and is caused by the expansion of a CTG repeat tract in the 3'-UTR of the DMPK gene.
evidence.explanation: Existing canonical mechanism citation in the dismech knowledge base, used as the seed for the hypothesis-search deep-research run.

evidence.snippet: Co-expression of SaCas9 and selected pairs of single-guide RNAs (sgRNAs) in cultured DM1 patient-derived muscle line cells carrying 2,600 CTG repeats resulted in targeted DNA deletion, ribonucleoprotein foci disappearance, and correction of splicing abnormalities in various transcripts.
evidence.explanation: DNA-level sufficiency test of the canonical axis: excising the expanded repeat from the DMPK locus in patient-derived muscle cells abolishes the ribonucleoprotein foci and corrects the spliceopathy, so the repeat is the upstream cause of both.

evidence.snippet: overexpression of Mbnl1 in vivo mediated by transduction of skeletal muscle with a recombinant adeno-associated viral vector rescues disease-associated muscle hyperexcitability, or myotonia, in the HSA(LR) poly(CUG) mouse model for DM
evidence.explanation: The gain-of-function half of the bidirectional genetic proof: restoring MBNL1 in the presence of an unchanged CUG-repeat burden reverses myotonia and adult splicing patterns, which places MBNL1 titration on the causal path rather than beside it.

hypotheses/0.description: Myotonic dystrophy type 1 (DM1) is caused by CTG-trinucleotide repeat expansion (>50 repeats; severe congenital >1000) in the 3' UTR of DMPK on 19q13.3. Expanded CUG-repeat RNA transcripts form nuclear foci that sequester MBNL1 (muscleblind-like 1) splicing factor and induce aberrant upregulation of CELF1, producing dysregulated alternative splicing of >100 developmentally regulated transcripts (e.g., CLCN1, INSR, SCN5A, BIN1). Mis-splicing reverts adult-tissue isoforms toward embryonic patterns, producing myotonia (CLCN1), insulin resistance (INSR), cardiac conduction defects (SCN5A), muscle weakness and atrophy, cataracts, frontal balding, hypogonadism, and characteristic CNS involvement. CTG repeat instability drives intergenerational anticipation. MBNL transgenic rescue, CUG-ASO therapy, and small-molecule MBNL/CELF1 normalizers corroborate the RNA-toxicity / splicing-dysregulation axis as the canonical pathogenic mechanism.

evidence.snippet: We showed that correction Scn5a mis-splicing does not improve the DM1 heart conduction delays and structural changes induced by CUG repeat RNA expression.
evidence.explanation: Establishes that the gap is real by showing a complete single-target splicing rescue with no cardiac benefit.

evidence.snippet: Sustained CUGexp RNA expression caused progressive cardiac enlargement, contractile dysfunction, conduction delay, myocardial fibrosis, and reduced survival, while MBNL-dependent splicing defects remained static, consistent with the stable repeat length.
evidence.explanation: Separates cardiac progression from both spliceopathy severity and somatic expansion, leaving the mediating step unaccounted for.

open_questions/0.rationale: Cardiac disease is a leading cause of death in DM1, and two independent mouse results say the splicing account of it is incomplete. Correcting the best-characterized cardiac splicing defect rescues nothing, and a repeat-length-stable model progresses to fibrosis, contractile failure, and death with splicing readouts unchanged. Whatever mediates that progression is unidentified, which means the current generation of splicing-directed and repeat-directed therapies has no established mechanism of action against the phenotype that kills patients. Candidate intermediates raised but not tested include reduced SCN5A expression as distinct from mis-splicing, fibrotic signaling, and cumulative cardiomyocyte loss.

evidence.snippet: A high proportion, 83% in DM1 and 75% in DM2, of the significantly disregulated genes were shared by both forms of the disease, suggesting a common mechanism.
evidence.explanation: The DM1/DM2 overlap is what makes the innate-immune branch a candidate independent of the DMPK locus, and so a genuine competitor to the SIX5 explanation rather than a restatement of it.

evidence.snippet: Since both the hyper-stimulation of K(+) efflux and cell death were reduced by the highly specific SK inhibitor apamin, we suggest that increased expression of SK3 has a critical role in the increased Ca(2+)-induced fragility in DM1 cells.
evidence.explanation: Gives the competing branch a pharmacologically demonstrated effector in human DM1 lens cells, which is why the relative contributions cannot be settled from the existing data.

open_questions/1.rationale: Cataract is near-universal in DM1 and the entry now carries two candidate lens mechanisms that are neither ranked nor mutually exclusive, alongside the splicing axis that explains the rest of the disease. Each rests on evidence of a different kind and none is decisive: the SIX5 branch has a mouse dosage series plus human lens cell lines in which SIX5 is measured but not manipulated, and the innate-immune branch has an expression signature in surgical specimens with no perturbation and no MBNL1 comparison arm. Because the lens is accessible and both DM1 and DM2 share the immune signature, this is an unusually tractable place to test whether repeat-RNA diseases have one mechanism hierarchy or tissue-specific ones.

evidence.snippet: The triple heterozygous mutant mice exhibit adult-onset DM1 phenotypes. With the additional mutation in Dmwd, the quadruple heterozygous mutant mice recapitulate many major manifestations in congenital DM1.
evidence.explanation: Records the model result whose translational validity is the open question. The authors demonstrate sufficiency of combined dosage reduction in mouse; no human congenital DM1 tissue has been shown to reproduce this dosage pattern.

open_questions/2.rationale: The mouse genetics are clean: triple heterozygous Dmpk, Six5 and Mbnl1 mutants show adult-onset DM1 phenotypes, and adding Dmwd yields quadruple heterozygotes recapitulating much of congenital DM1. But the construct is four engineered null alleles, whereas a human congenital DM1 patient has one expanded repeat and no null alleles at all. The experiment therefore shows that combined dosage reduction is sufficient to produce the phenotype, not that it is what happens in patients. The distinction matters for therapy: if congenital severity is dosage-driven at neighbouring loci, then removing or silencing the toxic RNA would not address it, whereas if it is repeat-driven through chromatin change at the locus, it would.

evidence.snippet: Myotonia reversal occurs concurrently with restoration of the normal adult-splicing patterns of four pre-mRNAs that are misspliced during postnatal development in DM muscle.
evidence.explanation: Establishes that restoration works and that splicing correction tracks the functional readout, which is what makes the missing quantitative threshold the actionable gap rather than the qualitative question.

open_questions/3.rationale: Restoring MBNL1 reverses myotonia and adult splicing in poly(CUG) mice, but the experiments that establish this use a single delivered dose and report an outcome, not a dose-response curve. No published work defines the fraction of normal MBNL1 activity that has to be recovered before a given tissue crosses back into a functional range, and the threshold is unlikely to be the same in skeletal muscle, heart, lens, and brain. That number is the therapeutic window for every approach in this class, and its absence is why the phase 1/2a DMPK ASO result — muscle exposure below the level predicted to reduce the target — could not be read as either a mechanism failure or a dosing failure.

evidence.snippet: NA onset was preceded by a symptomatic infectious trigger confirmed by microbiological tests in 15/57 (26.3%) patients.
evidence.explanation: The infection component, confirmed microbiologically rather than by history. Each case was matched to a healthy control for age, sex, residence and blood collection time, which is what distinguishes this from the uncontrolled series elsewhere in this entry.

evidence.snippet: An acute viral infection was associated with a bilateral involvement of the brachial plexus (p = 0.003, Cramèr's V = 0.43).
evidence.explanation: The trigger is associated with the anatomical pattern of the attack, not only with its occurrence. Quoted with the paper's own spelling of the statistic's name.

evidence.snippet: Coronavirus disease 2019 vaccination was considered a potential trigger in 7/57 (12.3%) subjects.
evidence.explanation: The vaccination component. The authors write "considered a potential trigger", which is weaker than the microbiologically confirmed infections above, and the wording is kept.

evidence.snippet: In all cases, O2C hepatitis genotype 3 was identified.
evidence.explanation: Identifies the genotype across the whole series, which is what makes this a specific exposure rather than "a viral illness".

evidence.snippet: Liver values were normal in all patients.
evidence.explanation: The reason the trigger is missed. By the time the neuropathy presents there is no hepatic signal to prompt HEV serology, so the exposure is only found when it is looked for.

evidence.snippet: Recurrences are common, yet the proposed multifactorial etiology, which includes genetic, biomechanical, and immunologic factors, limits our capacity to predict or prevent them.
evidence.explanation: States the three-component etiologic model and its practical consequence, which is why this node is marked provisional rather than established.

evidence.snippet: Autoimmune, genetic, infectious and mechanical processes are thought to be involved, but etiopathogenesis is still incompletely understood
evidence.explanation: An independent review reaching the same multifactorial conclusion and stating explicitly that the etiopathogenesis is not settled.

steps/2.description: Neuralgic amyotrophy is not attributed to a single initiating lesion. Genetic, biomechanical and immunologic factors are all implicated, and it is this multifactorial etiology - rather than a lack of study - that limits the ability to predict or prevent the recurrences that are common in this disease. The biomechanical component is what is thought to localise an otherwise systemic immune event to particular nerves.

evidence.snippet: There were florid multifocal mononuclear inflammatory cell infiltrates. Present evidence suggests that these brachial neuropathies have an immune basis.
evidence.explanation: Direct tissue evidence from brachial plexus biopsy in four patients, and the primary basis for the immune-mediated classification.

evidence.snippet: an auto-immune multifocal peripheral nervous system disorder that leaves many patients permanently impaired if not recognized and treated properly
evidence.explanation: Characterises the disorder as autoimmune and multifocal, and notes the cost of missing it.

evidence.snippet: which involves the perineurium and is associated with marked edema, a mononuclear inflammatory infiltration, composed of CD8-positive T lymphocytes
evidence.explanation: Identifies the effector cell population and the anatomical compartment of the lesion, which is what the cell-type and location bindings on this node record.

steps/3.description: Brachial plexus biopsy in affected patients shows florid multifocal mononuclear inflammatory cell infiltrates, which is the direct histopathological basis for calling the disorder immune-mediated. The infiltrate in the constricted segments is composed of CD8-positive T lymphocytes, and the lesion involves the perineurium with marked edema. "Multifocal" is doing real work here: the attack picks out individual nerves and even individual fascicles, which is why the resulting weakness is patchy rather than following a plexus territory.

evidence.snippet: the hourglass constriction, which is characterized by a very focal constriction of a nerve, or part of it, usually associated with nerve thickening proximally and distally to the constriction
evidence.explanation: Defines the structural lesion this node represents.

evidence.snippet: The prognosis of these conditions is often poor in the absence of any surgical treatment
evidence.explanation: Supports treating the constriction as a mechanistically distinct, surgically addressable lesion rather than a radiological curiosity.

steps/4.description: In a subset of patients the inflamed, swollen nerve develops a very focal constriction, with thickening proximal and distal to it, or frank torsion of the nerve or some of its fascicles. Ultrasound findings have been grouped as nerve swelling, swelling with incomplete constriction, swelling with complete constriction, and fascicular entwinement, which has been read as a continuum. The clinical importance is that these lesions do badly without surgery and well with it, so recognising them changes management.

evidence.snippet: usually a severe axonotmesis, documented during neurophysiological examination
evidence.explanation: Characterises the nerve injury as severe axonotmesis on electrophysiology.

steps/5.description: The affected nerves sustain axonal loss, typically a severe axonotmesis on neurophysiological testing. This produces the patchy paresis and, over weeks, the amyotrophy the disease is named for. Importantly the axonal damage is not the whole story of long-term disability - see the maladaptive motor pattern node downstream.

evidence.snippet: is characterised by sudden pain attacks, followed by patchy muscle paresis in the upper extremity
evidence.explanation: Establishes the defining temporal sequence of pain preceding patchy paresis, which the downstream edges of this entry encode.

steps/6.description: The illness opens with sudden, severe pain in the shoulder girdle. The pain is the presenting symptom and the window for immunomodulating treatment: it precedes the weakness, and it is while the patient is still in pain that corticosteroids are advised.

evidence.snippet: Long-term consequences are the rule, and persisting symptoms are mainly caused by a combination of decreased endurance in the affected nerves and an altered posture and movement pattern, not by the axonal damage itself.
evidence.explanation: States the claim directly, including the explicit negative - that axonal damage is not the main driver of persistent symptoms - which is the reason this node exists separately from the axonal injury node.

steps/7.description: The distinctive claim of the modern literature on this disease: persisting symptoms are caused mainly by a combination of decreased endurance in the affected nerves and an altered posture and movement pattern, and not by the axonal damage itself. This is why the long-term treatment target is scapular coordination and energy distribution rather than nerve regeneration, and why rehabilitation here is disease-modifying rather than supportive.

evidence.snippet: If patients are seen early and are still in pain, a short trial of high-dose oral corticosteroids is advised, and adequate analgesia may require opioids and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs.
evidence.explanation: Establishes pain as the early clinical state that defines the treatment window and characterises its severity by the analgesia required.

steps/8.description: Sudden, severe pain in the shoulder girdle opening the illness, before any weakness is apparent. Adequate analgesia may require opioids as well as NSAIDs.

evidence.snippet: is characterised by sudden pain attacks, followed by patchy muscle paresis in the upper extremity
evidence.explanation: Reports the patchy distribution of the weakness directly.

steps/9.description: Patchy paresis of the upper extremity following the pain. The patchiness reflects the multifocal nature of the nerve attack rather than a single plexus lesion.

evidence.snippet: in its classic presentation is a brachial plexopathy or a multifocal neuropathy, involving mainly motor nerves of the upper limb with a monophasic course
evidence.explanation: Supports the predominantly motor, upper-limb distribution that determines which muscles waste. Indirect for the atrophy itself, which the source names only in the disease term.

steps/10.description: Wasting of the denervated shoulder-girdle and upper limb muscles, the amyotrophy in the disease name, developing over weeks after the axonal injury.

evidence.snippet: a multidisciplinary rehabilitation approach focusing on scapular coordination, energy distribution strategies, and self-management is indicated
evidence.explanation: Scapular coordination being the named rehabilitation target establishes scapular dysfunction as a core persisting problem. Indirect: the source prescribes the treatment rather than describing the sign.

steps/11.description: Abnormal scapular position and movement, both from weakness of the periscapular muscles and from the altered movement pattern that develops afterwards. It is the specific target of the rehabilitation strategy.

evidence.snippet: Phrenic nerve involvement occurs in 8% of all NA patients, often with debilitating consequences.
evidence.explanation: Gives both the frequency and the clinical weight of phrenic involvement.

steps/12.description: Phrenic nerve involvement occurs in 8% of patients and is often debilitating. It is called out separately in the literature because identifying it early matters for recovery.

evidence.snippet: sometimes preceded by paraesthesias in the territory of the involved nerve (in the case of a mixed nerve) and pain
evidence.explanation: Documents paresthesia and its timing relative to the deficit. Note this sentence supports that paresthesia occurs and carries no frequency at all - the FREQUENT band comes from the cohort figure below, not from here.

evidence.snippet: Sensory involvement was quite common and found in 78.4% of patients but was clinically less impairing than the initial pain and subsequent paresis.
evidence.explanation: The frequency source. 78.4% falls in the FREQUENT band (30-79%). Note the denominator is the whole 246-patient series, which includes 47 hereditary cases alongside 199 idiopathic ones, so the figure is not purely of the acquired form this entry scopes to; the paper reports no separate sensory-involvement rate by subtype.

steps/13.description: Sensory symptoms in the territory of an affected mixed nerve, sometimes preceding the motor deficit. The disease is predominantly but not exclusively motor.

evidence.snippet: Over one third of the individual patients suffered from severe fatigue.
evidence.explanation: The frequency source, from 89 patients assessed on average two years after their last attack. Graded FREQUENT (30-79%) on "over one third" for severe fatigue; the same paper reports a quarter to a third with significant long-term fatigue on the looser criterion.

evidence.snippet: There was no correlation of pain or fatigue with the level of residual paresis on a Medical Research Council scale
evidence.explanation: The reason this phenotype is wired to the endurance node rather than to axonal injury: fatigue tracks neither with how weak the patient is nor with psychological distress, which is the dissociation the endurance model predicts.

steps/14.description: Persistent fatigue is one of the two dominant residual symptoms, alongside pain, and is the clinical readout of this entry's central mechanistic claim: it is not explained by residual paresis. The cohort study found no correlation between fatigue and the level of residual weakness on the MRC scale, which is the observation that separates this from simple deconditioning after nerve injury, and which is why the long-term treatment target is energy distribution rather than strength.

evidence.snippet: Confirmed immune triggers (infection or vaccination) preceded disease onset in 22/57 (38.6%) NA cases.
evidence.explanation: The headline figure from the only matched case-control study of triggers in this disease, with serology performed centrally rather than relying on patient report.

edges/13.description: An antecedent immune challenge precipitates the multifocal inflammatory attack in a susceptible plexus.

evidence.snippet: NA that shows involvement of the phrenic nerve resulting in diaphragmatic dysfunction and dyspnoea, may be associated with HEV infection
evidence.explanation: States the association and the phrenic predilection that makes it recognisable. Note the authors' own hedge - "may be associated" - which is why this edge is a trigger rather than a cause.

evidence.snippet: The diagnosis of neuralgic amyotrophy with diaphragmatic paralysis secondary to HEV was made
evidence.explanation: A single worked case with serology, viral load and electrodiagnostic confirmation of phrenic involvement.

edges/14.description: Infection precipitates the immune attack on the plexus, with a predilection for the phrenic nerve that distinguishes HEV-triggered attacks from other precipitants.

evidence.snippet: If patients are seen early and are still in pain, a short trial of high-dose oral corticosteroids is advised
evidence.explanation: States the recommendation and the timing constraint on it.

evidence.snippet: treatment options were confined to application of corticosteroids and symptomatic management, without proven positive effects on long-term outcomes
evidence.explanation: Refutes a long-term outcome benefit for corticosteroids. Recorded alongside the recommendation because the two claims are both true and about different endpoints: acute phase practice versus proven long-term effect.

treatments/0.description: A short trial of high-dose oral corticosteroids in the acute phase, advised for patients seen early while still in pain. The aim is to damp the inflammatory attack during the window in which it is still active.

evidence.snippet: The median time until initial pain relief was lower in the study group (12.5 days vs 20.5 days), and a significantly higher percentage already recovered strength in the first month of treatment (18% vs 6.3%; p = 0.011).
evidence.explanation: The comparative data behind the recommendation: 50 treated patients against a historical control group of 203 untreated ones. A retrospective case series with a historical control is weak for causal attribution, and the authors say so themselves - they recommend the regimen "pending a prospective, randomised trial verifying the results".

treatments/0/targets/0.description: Suppresses the acute inflammatory attack on the nerve during the painful phase.

evidence.snippet: Acute phase treatment of NA with steroids or i.v. immunoglobulin may benefit patients.
evidence.explanation: Names IVIG as an acute-phase option. The hedged "may benefit" is the strength of the claim and is not upgraded here.

treatments/1.description: Immunomodulating treatment in the acute phase, cited alongside steroids as potentially beneficial. Early immunomodulation is presented as important for optimal recovery.

treatments/1/targets/0.description: Immunomodulation directed at the acute immune attack on the nerve.

evidence.snippet: surgery has shown to improve clinical outcomes in such cases, indicating the viability of peripheral nerve surgery as a valuable treatment option in NA
evidence.explanation: Supports surgery for the imaging-identified constriction subgroup specifically.

evidence.snippet: The prognosis is generally favorable after surgery, with a high rate of good motor recovery.
evidence.explanation: Independent statement of post-surgical outcome in the constriction subgroup.

evidence.snippet: Nine of 11 operative patients experienced clinical recovery compared with 3 of 13 nonsurgical patients.
evidence.explanation: The comparative outcome behind the recommendation, quoted as counts rather than as a percentage because the arms are 11 and 13 patients. The paper grades itself Therapeutic IV, and allocation was not randomised, so this establishes an association between surgery and recovery in a selected group, not an effect size.

treatments/2.description: Surgical treatment of hourglass constrictions and nerve torsion identified on high-resolution imaging. This is the treatment that the structural findings made possible, and it applies to the constriction subgroup rather than to neuralgic amyotrophy generally.

treatments/2/targets/0.description: Addresses the focal structural lesion directly, by neurolysis, resection or grafting of the constricted segment.

evidence.snippet: Common etiologies of phrenic injuries include cervical trauma, iatrogenic injury in the neck or chest, and neuralgic amyotrophy.
evidence.explanation: Establishes that neuralgic amyotrophy is among the phrenic injuries this operation is performed for, which is what makes the treatment in scope for this entry.

evidence.snippet: Surgical repair of the nerve injury to restore functional diaphragmatic activity, termed phrenic nerve reconstruction, is a safe and effective alternative to static repositioning of the diaphragm (diaphragm plication), in properly selected patients.
evidence.explanation: The efficacy claim, with the authors' own restriction to "properly selected patients" preserved. A review statement, not a trial result.

treatments/3.description:
Surgical repair of the injured phrenic nerve for symptomatic diaphragm paralysis, in selected patients. Curated because diaphragmatic weakness is a phenotype of this entry with no other treatment linked to it, and because it is the intervention that follows from the HEV-associated phrenic presentation.
The evidence is weaker than for the other surgical entry here: this is a narrative review of phrenic nerve reconstruction across all causes of phrenic injury, of which neuralgic amyotrophy is one, not a series of NA patients. It reports no NA-specific outcome.

treatments/3/targets/0.description: Restores functional diaphragmatic activity by repairing the nerve lesion, rather than compensating for it mechanically as diaphragm plication does.

evidence.snippet: Persistent complaints are common, and a multidisciplinary rehabilitation approach focusing on scapular coordination, energy distribution strategies, and self-management is indicated.
evidence.explanation: States the indication and the specific content of the rehabilitation programme.

evidence.snippet: Patients benefit from specific rehabilitation treatment.
evidence.explanation: Independent statement of benefit from targeted rehabilitation.

evidence.snippet: The mean group difference adjusted for sex, age and SRQ-DLV baseline score was 8.60 (95%CI: 0.26 to 16.94, p=0.044).
evidence.explanation: The primary outcome of the only randomised trial of this intervention, and the strongest interventional evidence in this disease. Note the confidence interval nearly touches zero and the trial randomised 47 patients but analysed 37 after dropout, so the effect is real but imprecise.

evidence.snippet: The proportion attaining a minimal clinically relevant SRQ-DLV improvement (≥12) was larger for the MR group (59%) than the UC group (33%) with a number needed to treat of 4.
evidence.explanation: The responder analysis, which is what makes the effect interpretable: a number needed to treat of 4 on a clinically anchored threshold rather than a group mean on a scale.

evidence.snippet: rather than strength training which may worsen the symptoms
evidence.explanation: The explicit negative that defines the intervention by contrast. Curated because the obvious rehabilitation approach to a weak limb is the wrong one here, and an entry that records only what to do leaves that trap in place.

treatments/4.description: Multidisciplinary rehabilitation focused on scapular coordination, energy distribution strategies and self-management. Because persisting symptoms are attributed to reduced nerve endurance and an altered movement pattern rather than to axon loss, this targets the actual driver of long-term disability and is not merely supportive.

treatments/4/targets/0.description: Retrains scapular coordination and paces energy expenditure, addressing the movement pattern and endurance limitation that carry the persisting symptoms.

evidence.snippet: The pathophysiology of neuralgic amyotrophy, hourglass constriction and nerve torsion is still poorly understood, and a generic role of inflammation is proposed for all these conditions.
evidence.explanation: States that the shared mechanism is proposed rather than demonstrated, which is the basis for recording this as a controversy.

evidence.snippet: in some cases of NA, after a first phase characterized by nerve inflammation and swelling, in selected anatomical conditions, the process evolves into hourglass constriction or nerve torsion
evidence.explanation: The continuum hypothesis in its explicit form, which is the reading the pathograph currently encodes.

open_questions/0.rationale: This is stated as an open question in the review literature rather than a settled point, and it has direct consequences for this entry's structure. If they are one process, the constriction node belongs downstream of the inflammatory attack, which is how the pathograph currently draws it, and the ultrasound categories - swelling, swelling with incomplete constriction, swelling with complete constriction, fascicular entwinement - are stages of a continuum. If they are separate entities, that edge is wrong and the constriction cases are a different disease that happens to look similar. The node carries mechanism_confidence: PROVISIONAL for this reason - causal_link_type records directness, not confidence, so it is not the slot that expresses this. The practical stakes are not academic: the constriction subgroup has a poor prognosis without surgery and a good one with it, so which patients are considered to have "neuralgic amyotrophy" determines who gets referred.

evidence.snippet: These findings provide evidence for an obligate dependency on proper NRAS function in human development and growth.
evidence.explanation: Establishes that constitutional perturbation of NRAS function is the causal lesion in this developmental disorder.

evidence.snippet: Here, we report a mutation in NRAS, resulting in an I24N amino acid substitution, that we identified in an individual bearing typical Noonan syndrome features.
evidence.explanation: First-party identification of a germline NRAS substitution in an individual with typical Noonan syndrome features, extending the allelic spectrum of this subtype.

evidence.snippet: Importantly, four of them harbored missense changes affecting Gly12, which was previously described to occur exclusively in cancer.
evidence.explanation: Documents that germline NS6 alleles extend to the classic somatic oncogenic codon Gly12, contradicting the earlier "restricted spectrum" model.

evidence.snippet: Of note, the G60E NRAS mutant, much like G12V, accumulated constitutively in the active, GTP-bound form and appeared resistant to GAP stimulation. In contrast, the T50I NRAS mutant was not enriched in the GTP-bound state (Fig. 2d,e), indicating a different mechanism of functional dysregulation.
evidence.explanation: Cellular assays distinguish G60E accumulation/GAP resistance from T50I signaling without increased GTP loading.

evidence.snippet:
By contrast, ectopic expression
of either NRAS Thr58Ile or NRASGly12Val promoted enhanced activation
of ERK and AKT, even in absence of stimulation (Figure 2a).
evidence.explanation: Transiently transfected HEK293T cells show basal ERK and AKT activation by Thr58Ile and Gly12Val; stimulus dependence cannot be generalized.

steps/1.description: Heterozygous germline NRAS variants increase signaling through allele-dependent mechanisms. Gly60Glu resists GAP stimulation and accumulates in the GTP-bound state; Thr50Ile enhances signaling without increased GTP loading, with altered membrane orientation proposed. Ile24Asn may alter nucleotide affinity, whereas Thr58Ile and oncogenic Gly12 variants can increase basal signaling. Thus increased nucleotide exchange and stimulus dependence are not universal. Constitutional origin should be assessed in non-hematopoietic tissue because NRAS is also a somatic oncogene.

evidence.snippet: Although infants with Noonan syndrome are predisposed to several haematological abnormalities, including transient monocytosis, thrombocytopenia, and myeloproliferative disorder,26 the most common haematologic disorders are abnormalities of bleeding caused by coagulation defects.
evidence.explanation: Noonan-wide causal relationship between hemostatic defects and bleeding; the NRAS cohort identifies a confirmed coagulopathy in only one individual.

steps/2.description: Coagulation-factor or platelet abnormalities can produce bleeding in Noonan syndrome. In the NRAS series, von Willebrand disease was confirmed in one of the three individuals with bleeding; the other two had no defined coagulopathy. This node represents a contributing mechanism, without assuming that NRAS directly caused von Willebrand disease.

evidence.snippet: The I24N mutation activates N-Ras, resulting in enhanced downstream signaling.
evidence.explanation: Functional demonstration that a Noonan-associated germline NRAS substitution activates the protein and increases downstream signalling.

evidence.snippet: Therefore, it is not surprising that Ras/MAPK pathway dysregulation has profound deleterious effects on both embryonic and later stages of development.
evidence.explanation: Review-level interpretation that Ras/MAPK dysregulation disrupts development across the RASopathies. Its application to the NRAS subtype is indirect; it is not a clinical observation from an NRAS cohort.

steps/3.description: The activated N-Ras protein drives excessive signalling through the RAF-MEK-ERK (MAPK) cascade — the shared final common mechanism of the RASopathies. Enhanced ERK output during embryonic and postnatal development perturbs proliferation, differentiation and survival across multiple lineages, producing the multisystem Noonan phenotype.

evidence.snippet:
By contrast, ectopic expression
of either NRAS Thr58Ile or NRASGly12Val promoted enhanced activation
of ERK and AKT, even in absence of stimulation (Figure 2a).
evidence.explanation: Transiently transfected HEK293T cells expressing Thr58Ile or Gly12Val show increased basal AKT phosphorylation. This supports a parallel PI3K-AKT effector arm for these tested alleles, not uniform activation by all NRAS variants.

steps/4.description: Enhanced basal AKT phosphorylation accompanies ERK activation in HEK293T cells expressing NRAS Thr58Ile or Gly12Val. This experimentally supported parallel effector response does not establish which human NS6 phenotypes depend on PI3K-AKT or that every germline allele has the same effect.

evidence.snippet: Endothelial/endocardial-specific expression of NrasG12D/ + caused the cardiac morphological defects and embryonic lethality as observed in NrasG12D/ + ; Mox2Cre/ + mutants, but myocardial-specific expression of NrasG12D/ + did not.
evidence.explanation: Localizes the cardiac requirement for activated N-Ras to the endocardial/endothelial compartment, not the myocardium.

steps/5.description: Embryonic NrasG12D activation disrupts cardiac morphogenesis in mice. Endothelial/endocardial expression recapitulates ventricular septal and pulmonary valve defects; cardiomyocyte-specific expression does not. These experiments support a candidate route for structural NS6 lesions, but do not explain human HCM: the mutant mouse myocardium is thin, and transfer across alleles, dosage and species remains uncertain.

evidence.snippet: A spectrum of complex anomalies such as enlargement of lymphatic channels (lymphangiectasia), dysmotility, or central conducting lymphatic anomaly (CCLA) cause inadequate clearing of lymph with resultant stasis and reflux, affecting various organ systems, and resulting in lymphedema, chylothorax, pericardial effusion, congenital pulmonary lymphangiectasia (CPL), exudative enteropathy, chylous ascites, cystic hygroma, hydrops and other manifestations, some of which are detectable as early as the second trimester of pregnancy and are potentially life-threatening in neonates (12–14).
evidence.explanation: Review-level mechanism in Noonan syndrome: impaired lymph clearance, stasis and reflux cause these fluid findings. Applied indirectly to NRAS-associated lymphatic manifestations.

steps/6.description: Developmentally abnormal lymphatic channels and transport can impair lymph clearance, causing stasis, reflux and fluid accumulation. RAS-MAPK-driven lymphatic proliferation is established in other Noonan models; applying the route to NRAS disease is provisional. Prenatal lymphatic distension is also a published hypothesis for selected facial, neck and genital findings, rather than their proven universal cause.

evidence.snippet: Expression of N-Ras-I24N, N-Ras-G60E or the strongly activating mutant N-Ras-G12V, which we included as a positive control, results in developmental defects in zebrafish embryos, demonstrating that these activating N-Ras mutants are sufficient to induce developmental disorders.
evidence.explanation: Establishes sufficiency of the Noonan-associated N-Ras mutants to cause early developmental defects in vivo.

steps/7.description: Noonan-associated activating N-Ras mutants are sufficient to derail early morphogenesis. In zebrafish, expression of the human NS-derived I24N and G60E mutants causes gastrulation defects phenocopying those of other Noonan syndrome genes, indicating that the germline lesion acts on early embryonic patterning rather than only on postnatal growth.
