evidence.snippet: Additionally, the specific p.G12R NRAS mutation in this case is a common somatic mutation in cancer cells, and analysis of previously reported NRAS-RASopathy cases suggests that mutations at traditionally oncogenic codons are associated with elevated cancer risk not present with mutations at other sites.
evidence.explanation: States the codon-dependent tumor-risk pattern that motivates this node.

evidence.snippet: Further, one of the patients (c.35G>A; p.(Gly12Asp)) had a myeloproliferative disorder, and one subject (c.34G>C; p.(Gly12Arg)) exhibited an uncharacterized brain tumour.
evidence.explanation: The NRAS cohort reports a JMML-like myeloproliferative disorder in a p.Gly12Asp infant and an uncharacterized hypothalamic mass in a p.Gly12Arg infant. The latter was proposed to be a hamartoma or lipoma without biopsy, so these are not two confirmed neoplastic events.

evidence.snippet: Neither of affected individuals in this family presented with juvenile myelomonocytic leukemia (JMML), which together with previously published results suggest that the risk for NS individuals with a germline NRAS mutation developing JMML is not different from the proportion seen in other NS cases.
evidence.explanation: Counterweight to a blanket high-risk reading: JMML risk in NRAS-positive Noonan syndrome is not reported as elevated above Noonan syndrome generally.

steps/8.description: Germline NRAS substitutions at oncogenic codons, notably Gly12, may increase tumor susceptibility. Case reports include embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma and JMML-like myeloproliferation; an unbiopsied hypothalamic mass may instead be a hamartoma or lipoma. The authors propose allele-dependent risk, but small, age-heterogeneous series do not establish absolute risk or absence of risk for non-hotspot alleles.

evidence.snippet: Affected individuals exhibited features fitting Noonan syndrome, and the observed germline variants differed from the typical oncogenic NRAS changes occurring as somatic events in tumours.
evidence.explanation: Establishes that individuals with germline NRAS variants present with the Noonan syndrome clinical gestalt.

evidence.snippet: Noonan syndrome, a developmental disorder characterized by congenital heart defects, reduced growth, facial dysmorphism and variable cognitive deficits, is caused by constitutional dysregulation of the RAS-MAPK signaling pathway.
evidence.explanation: Facial dysmorphism is named as a defining feature of the disorder in the paper that established NRAS as a cause - but this sentence is the paper's background definition of Noonan syndrome as a whole rather than a finding about its NRAS cohort, so it is graded INDIRECT on the same basis as the GeneReviews parent-entity statements elsewhere in this entry.

steps/9.description: The characteristic RASopathy face — hypertelorism, downslanting palpebral fissures, ptosis, and low-set posteriorly rotated ears — evolving with age. It is the feature that identifies affected individuals clinically as having Noonan syndrome before molecular testing.

evidence.snippet: Because of the common underlying Ras/MAPK pathway dysregulation, the RASopathies exhibit numerous overlapping phenotypic features.

evidence.snippet: MEK inhibition completely rescued the activated N-Ras-induced phenotypes, demonstrating that these defects are mediated exclusively by Ras-MAPK signaling.

edges/8.description: Activated N-Ras signalling perturbs early embryonic morphogenetic movements; MEK inhibition fully reverses the effect, establishing that the defect is MAPK-mediated.

evidence.snippet:
Nuchal oedema and fetal chylothorax/hydrops as prenatal
abnormalities were seen in 15 and 23%, respectively.
evidence.explanation: Documents the NRAS-associated prenatal finding whose provisional lymphatic mechanism is supplied by the separate Noonan review.

edges/29.description: Impaired prenatal lymph drainage provides a provisional explanation for localized nuchal fluid accumulation. The general Noonan lymphatic mechanism is extrapolated to fetal nuchal edema observed in NRAS cases; its precise anatomic defect is not established.

evidence.snippet: Although infants with Noonan syndrome are predisposed to several haematological abnormalities, including transient monocytosis, thrombocytopenia, and myeloproliferative disorder,26 the most common haematologic disorders are abnormalities of bleeding caused by coagulation defects.
evidence.explanation: Noonan-wide causal relationship between hemostatic defects and bleeding; the NRAS cohort identifies a confirmed coagulopathy in only one individual.

edges/30.description: A documented coagulopathy contributes to bleeding in a subset; causal attribution of the coagulopathy to NRAS itself remains uncertain.

evidence.snippet: Here we report that germline NRAS mutations conferring enhanced stimulus-dependent MAPK activation account for some cases of this disorder.
evidence.explanation: The enhanced MAPK activation component of this claim derives from transfected-cell assays; human sequencing establishes the germline diagnosis.

evidence.snippet: NRAS | HGNC:7989 | Noonan syndrome | MONDO:0018997 | AD | Definitive
evidence.explanation: ClinGen's RASopathy Gene Curation Expert Panel classifies the NRAS-Noonan syndrome relationship as Definitive with autosomal dominant inheritance.

evidence.snippet: The phenotype associated with germline NRAS mutations is variable. Our results confirm that a small proportion of Noonan syndrome patients carry germline NRAS mutations.
evidence.explanation: Supports both the rarity of the NRAS subtype and its variable expressivity.

genes/0.notes: NRAS encodes the canonical small GTPase N-Ras. NS6 is caused by heterozygous germline missense gain-of-function variants; reported residues include Ile24, Thr50, Thr58, Gly60 and the classic somatic oncogenic codon Gly12. Cohort screens place NRAS at a very small share of molecularly solved Noonan syndrome (3/115 and 2/125 in two mutation-negative screening cohorts). ClinGen's RASopathy expert panel classifies the NRAS-Noonan syndrome relationship as Definitive with autosomal dominant inheritance. Constitutional status must be confirmed in non-hematopoietic tissue when an oncogenic-hotspot allele is found in blood during a myeloid-neoplasia workup.

evidence.snippet: Growth hormone (GH) treatment increases growth velocity.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews summarizes increased growth velocity with GH treatment in Noonan syndrome. Applied indirectly because the reported treatment effect is not specific to NRAS.

evidence.snippet:
Her FH is 164.5 cm ( −0.45 SDS) and weight of 60 kg (+0.3
SDS).
evidence.explanation: Final height in the p.G60E woman following childhood GH treatment; the preceding case history documents treatment and partial GH deficiency.

evidence.snippet:
She had low endogenous growth hormone (GH) secretion
defined as “partial GH deficiency”, and started GH therapy
within a formal clinical trial (NovoNordisk) from 6.5 years
of age. She was treated with GH (dose of 66 μg/kg/day)
and responded exceptionally well and treatment was dis-
continued after two years.
evidence.explanation: The p.G60E woman received GH and had an excellent response; a single patient cannot quantify subtype-wide effectiveness.

treatments/0.description: Growth hormone can increase growth velocity in Noonan syndrome. One p.G60E woman with partial GH deficiency had an excellent childhood response and reached 164.5 cm; this single case does not establish average NS6 efficacy or long-term safety.

evidence.snippet: A short-term improvement of symptoms was reported in all cases, with three deaths presumably unrelated to trametinib. Moderate side effects were reported in a subset of patients. Long-term follow-up data were not available.
evidence.explanation: Systematic review of off-label trametinib in severe Noonan syndrome. Graded INDIRECT because the collected cases are Noonan syndrome generally (the index case was PTPN11), not NRAS-associated NS6.

evidence.snippet: No formal clinical trial of trametinib in neonatal/pediatric Noonan syndrome has been published to our knowledge.
evidence.explanation: The authors describe the published literature as of their review, not an observed treatment outcome. This supports the experimental status of trametinib in general Noonan syndrome and applies indirectly to NRAS-associated NS6.

treatments/1.description: MEK1/2 inhibition targets the step of the RAS-MAPK cascade immediately downstream of the activated N-Ras protein, and MEK inhibition fully rescues the developmental phenotypes of Noonan-associated N-Ras mutants in zebrafish. In humans it remains off-label and experimental, used in case reports for severe cardiac and lymphatic disease in Noonan syndrome; no NS6-specific outcome data exist and long-term follow-up is unavailable.

evidence.snippet: MEK inhibition completely rescued the activated N-Ras-induced phenotypes, demonstrating that these defects are mediated exclusively by Ras-MAPK signaling.
evidence.explanation: Establishes MEK as the actionable node downstream of Noonan-associated activated N-Ras.

treatments/1/targets/0.description: MEK1/2 inhibition blocks signal flow through the hyperactivated cascade downstream of the mutant N-Ras protein.

evidence.snippet: Cardiovascular anomalies in NS are usually treated as in the general population.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews management guidance for the parent entity. Graded INDIRECT because it is not NRAS-specific.

treatments/2.description: Cardiovascular anomalies are treated as in the general population, with scheduled echocardiographic surveillance because hypertrophic cardiomyopathy may appear after infancy.

evidence.snippet: Agents/circumstances to avoid: Aspirin therapy should be avoided because it may exacerbate a bleeding diathesis.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews drug-safety warning for Noonan syndrome. Graded INDIRECT because it applies to the parent entity.

treatments/3.description: Because varied coagulation defects occur, bleeding history and coagulation testing are assessed before surgery, and aspirin therapy is avoided as it may exacerbate the bleeding diathesis.

evidence.snippet: Each child of an individual with autosomal dominant NS has a 50% chance of inheriting the pathogenic variant.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews recurrence-risk statement underpinning counseling. Graded INDIRECT because it is a parent-entity statement.

treatments/4.description: Counseling covers the 50% transmission risk from an affected parent, the predominance of de novo events, and the residual recurrence risk from parental mosaicism. Constitutional versus somatic origin must be clarified when an oncogenic-hotspot NRAS allele is detected in blood.

evidence.snippet: Clinical exam remains the mainstay of early intervention, and all patients, regardless of genotype, are recommended to have close monitoring including physical examination for hepatosplenomegaly especially during infancy and early childhood (Table 2).
evidence.explanation: The AACR consensus recommends clinical monitoring across Noonan genotypes, including NRAS by scope. This is expert advice rather than an NRAS-specific surveillance-outcome study.

evidence.snippet: There is no evidence that in otherwise healthy children with NS or CBL syndrome, surveillance with complete blood counts (CBC) is beneficial. Therefore, routine CBC has been removed from surveillance, in alignment with other CPS predisposing to leukemia (See related manuscript through the AACR-Cancer Predisposition Working Group specific to leukemia surveillance).
evidence.explanation: Routine blood-count screening is not recommended for healthy asymptomatic children. This does not apply to a child with suspected MPD, illness or hepatosplenomegaly.

evidence.snippet: Every 3 months through age 1y, then at every well child visit until age 5y, and as needed for clinical symptoms.
evidence.explanation: Table 2 starts monitoring at birth or diagnosis; CBC is indicated when ill or when hepatosplenomegaly is found, and abnormal findings warrant an experienced hematologist.

evidence.snippet: The absolute cancer risk for non-hematologic malignancies is not sufficiently high to warrant radiologic or laboratory surveillance. However, education of patients and families on the signs and symptoms of RMS, gliomas, and NB can be considered.
evidence.explanation: The consensus favors symptom education over routine solid-tumor imaging or laboratory screening in Noonan syndrome. It does not supply allele-specific NRAS penetrance estimates or a tumor-preventive treatment.

treatments/5.description: The 2024 AACR consensus recommends physical examination for hepatosplenomegaly from birth or diagnosis, every three months through age one year, then at each well-child visit until age five and as indicated by symptoms, regardless of Noonan genotype. Obtain a CBC for illness or hepatosplenomegaly and refer suspected MPD to pediatric hematology/oncology. Routine CBC in healthy asymptomatic children and routine imaging or laboratory surveillance for solid tumors are not recommended; families may receive symptom education. These are general Noonan recommendations applied to NS6, not NRAS-specific evidence of surveillance benefit.

evidence.snippet: analysis of previously reported NRAS-RASopathy cases suggests that mutations at traditionally oncogenic codons are associated with elevated cancer risk not present with mutations at other sites
evidence.explanation: The codon-dependent risk claim is explicitly hedged as a suggestion from reanalysis of previously reported cases, which is the gap this discussion records.

evidence.snippet: the risk for NS individuals with a germline NRAS mutation developing JMML is not different from the proportion seen in other NS cases
evidence.explanation: Historical interpretation from a small, earlier case series; it cannot establish risk equivalence or refute later allele-specific susceptibility.

open_questions/0.rationale: Published NRAS RASopathy series contain few tumor events with heterogeneous ages and follow-up. The 2015 familial literature review predates the expanded oncogenic-codon spectrum and cannot establish equal risk between NRAS and other Noonan genotypes. The 2017 brain mass was unbiopsied and possibly hamartomatous. Allele-stratified lifetime risk therefore remains unresolved.

evidence.snippet: Thus, oncogenic NrasG12D mutation may not be compatible with embryonic survival.
evidence.explanation: The authors' own conclusion that the modelled allele is embryonic-lethal is precisely the translational mismatch with living human NS6 individuals that this discussion records.

evidence.snippet: Expression of N-Ras-I24N, N-Ras-G60E or the strongly activating mutant N-Ras-G12V, which we included as a positive control, results in developmental defects in zebrafish embryos
evidence.explanation: The zebrafish readout comes from injected expression benchmarked against a strongly activating positive control, not from an endogenous heterozygous locus - the dosage mismatch this discussion records.

open_questions/1.rationale: The mouse model uses the oncogenic G12D allele expressed pan-embryonically and is lethal between E15.5 and E17.5, so it cannot model the postnatal NS6 course; the zebrafish model uses transient mRNA overexpression of human mutants rather than an endogenous heterozygous locus. Both give a clear MAPK-dependent developmental phenotype, but the quantitative relationship between their signalling gain and that of a human NS6 heterozygote is unknown - which matters directly for interpreting the MEK-inhibitor rescue as a therapeutic rationale.

evidence.snippet: Thus, it is conceivable that NRAS haploinsufficiency and gain-of-function mutations may have similar clinical consequences.
evidence.explanation: The authors state the convergence as a conjecture ("it is conceivable"), which is precisely why it is recorded here as an open question rather than as a competing mechanism in the pathograph.

evidence.snippet: Here we report that germline NRAS mutations conferring enhanced stimulus-dependent MAPK activation account for some cases of this disorder.
evidence.explanation: The enhanced MAPK activation component of this claim derives from transfected-cell assays; human sequencing establishes the germline diagnosis.

open_questions/2.rationale: The canonical MAPK interpretation of NS6 involves increased signal throughput into RAF-MEK-ERK. A loss-of-dosage lesion converging on a similar clinical picture challenges a simple monotonic MAPK model; it does not establish equivalence across the parallel effector responses, including AKT. Three readings are open and the published data do not separate them: the deletion phenotype may be driven by other genes in the deleted segment rather than by NRAS; reduced N-Ras may perturb pathway output non-monotonically, so that both raising and lowering it degrades developmental signalling; or the shared features may be non-specific enough that clinical overlap does not imply mechanistic convergence. The same loss-and-gain pattern is reported for MAP2K2 and SHOC2, so this is a recurring question about RAS-MAPK dosage rather than an NRAS curiosity. Resolving it bears on whether MEK inhibition is a rational therapy for the deletion phenotype, where it could plausibly make matters worse.

evidence.snippet:
Motor delay and
intellectual or learning disabilities were recorded in 38 and 42% of
patients, respectively.
evidence.explanation: The 2017 series comprises 19 individuals from 13 families with NRAS-associated RASopathy, including NS, CFCS-like and Costello-like presentations. Aggregate statistics exclude the patient with a 22q11.23 duplication and hypoxic ischemic encephalopathy; denominators vary with ascertainment.

evidence.snippet: We present the case of a germline heterozygous NRAS mutation producing a severe phenotype involving embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma, severe intellectual disability, and numerous melanocytic nevi in addition to more typical manifestations of Noonan syndrome.
evidence.explanation: Single reported case documenting severe intellectual disability in NRAS-associated RASopathy. No frequency band is asserted: the report supplies no denominator, so the proportion of NS6 individuals reaching this severity cannot be estimated from it.

open_questions/3.rationale: Motor delay and hypotonia are separable from intellect, and later catch-up is documented. The severe intellectual-disability case is allele-specific; the extreme 2017 Glu37dup developmental presentation also had a 22q11.23 duplication and hypoxic ischemic injury. The reviewed NRAS sources do not resolve the relative neural, muscular and sensory contributions. A specific causal tissue route for hearing loss is not established.

evidence.snippet: Expression of N-Ras-I24N led to a significant increase in the angle of the ceratohyal (P<0.05; Student’s t-test) (Fig. 4C,D) and hence we conclude that N-Ras-I24N expression induced craniofacial defects in zebrafish embryos that are reminiscent of the symptoms in individuals with Noonan syndrome.
evidence.explanation: Ceratohyal-angle changes in a transient-expression zebrafish model support craniofacial widening; translation to human hypertelorism is provisional.

evidence.snippet:
She has two large Café-au-lait spots on her back and >50
freckles (lentigines) all over her body, especially on her
back (Fig. 1b) and arms (Fig. 1c).
evidence.explanation: The same p.G60E woman had more than 50 lentigines and two large cafe-au-lait spots; these are separate findings.

open_questions/4.rationale: The reviewed sources establish the clinical findings but do not assign distinct tissue mechanisms to these endpoints. The zebrafish craniofacial evidence supports widening, not every facial feature; the NrasG12D mouse demonstrates ventricular septation and pulmonary valve defects, not a ductal mechanism; the atrial septal pathway link is instead a qualified extrapolation from the RASopathy review. Somatic mosaic NRAS nevus biology cannot automatically establish the mechanism of pigmentation in constitutional NS6. Pectus carinatum remains supported indirectly by parent-Noonan evidence. The clinical NRAS reports identify curly hair, sparse scalp hair and sparse eyebrows, but do not establish their follicular mechanism or demonstrate that the experimental AKT response causes these findings.

evidence.snippet:
The postnatal
period was complicated by prolonged hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia,
severe feeding dif ﬁculties, including oral aversion and respiratory
difﬁculties due to upper airway collapse. She was treated with a
percutaneous gastrostomy and a tracheostomy with continuous
positive airway pressure ventilation.
evidence.explanation: Patient 12 with p.Gly12Arg had prolonged postnatal hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia, severe feeding difficulties and upper-airway collapse. These co-occurring case-specific complications do not establish a single shared mechanism.

evidence.snippet:
In addition, the majority of patients had prenatal
abnormalities (69%) with polyhydramnios being reported in 46% of
the cases.
evidence.explanation: The 2017 series comprises 19 individuals from 13 families with NRAS-associated RASopathy, including NS, CFCS-like and Costello-like presentations. Aggregate statistics exclude the patient with a 22q11.23 duplication and hypoxic ischemic encephalopathy; denominators vary with ascertainment.

evidence.snippet:
Patient 13 — (c.35G4A, p.(Gly12Asp)) is a male born after an
uneventful pregnancy except for mild fetal pyelocalyceal dilatation
(7 mm) of the left kidney detected on ultrasound scans.
evidence.explanation: Prenatal mild unilateral renal pelvic/calyceal dilation in the p.Gly12Asp patient, independently of the confounded p.Glu37dup case with complex urinary abnormalities.

open_questions/5.rationale: The severe Gly12Arg presentation combines oral aversion, upper airway collapse and hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia, with subsequent improvement. Their co-occurrence does not identify the NRAS-dependent tissue route or establish that one causes the others. Polyhydramnios is documented separately from hydrops; the series does not identify a uniform mechanism. These are attribution gaps, not evidence that all findings are causally independent. The mild prenatal renal dilation likewise lacks a demonstrated NRAS-specific causal anatomical or functional route.

evidence.snippet:
A brain MRI at 8 months of
age revealed an expansive lesion of 0.8x0.7x0.6 cm in the hypothala-
mus proposed to represent a hamartoma or lipoma (Supplementary
Figure S2).
evidence.explanation: The report calls this a tumor-like lesion but proposes hamartoma or lipoma. This supports a suspected mass, not a histologically confirmed malignant brain tumor.

open_questions/6.rationale: The unbiopsied p.Gly12Arg hypothalamic mass was proposed to be a hamartoma or lipoma. The report discusses it alongside possible tumor predisposition, but its biological nature is unresolved. It is therefore not assigned an established causal tumor-predisposition edge.

evidence.snippet:
By contrast, ectopic expression
of either NRAS Thr58Ile or NRASGly12Val promoted enhanced activation
of ERK and AKT, even in absence of stimulation (Figure 2a).
evidence.explanation: Transiently transfected HEK293T cells expressing Thr58Ile or Gly12Val show increased basal AKT phosphorylation. This supports a parallel PI3K-AKT effector arm for these tested alleles, not uniform activation by all NRAS variants.

open_questions/7.rationale: Thr58Ile and Gly12Val increase basal AKT phosphorylation in an ectopic HEK293T expression assay. The study does not isolate AKT-dependent human developmental outcomes or show comparable activation across all germline NRAS alleles; clinical phenotype fanout therefore remains unresolved.

evidence.snippet: A total of 36% of patients with OSA had minimal genioglossus muscle responsiveness during sleep, 37% had a low arousal threshold, and 36% had high loop gain.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the three non-anatomic traits in a phenotyped cohort, which is the evidence that this node is a real and common contributor rather than a theoretical refinement.

evidence.snippet: In these patients, loop gain was almost twice as high as patients with a Pcrit greater than -2 cm H2O
evidence.explanation: Shows the trade-off between the anatomic and control arms directly: where the airway is comparatively non-collapsible, loop gain is roughly double.

evidence.snippet: This study confirms that OSA is a heterogeneous disorder. Although Pcrit-anatomy is an important determinant, abnormalities in nonanatomic traits are also present in most patients with OSA.
evidence.explanation: The study's own conclusion, and the reason this entry curates a non-anatomic node alongside the airway-collapse trigger rather than treating anatomy as the mechanism.

steps/0.description: Obstructive sleep apnoea is not one mechanism graded by severity. Careful physiological phenotyping identifies four largely independent contributing traits: pharyngeal collapsibility (the anatomic trait, measured as passive critical closing pressure), genioglossus muscle responsiveness during sleep, the arousal threshold, and respiratory control stability (loop gain). Around a third of patients each have minimal genioglossus responsiveness, a low arousal threshold, or high loop gain, and non-anatomic features contribute importantly in the majority. About one patient in five has a relatively non-collapsible airway similar to controls, and in those patients loop gain is roughly double - control instability substituting for anatomy. This node is curated because the apnoea-hypopnoea index by which the disease is graded is a count of events, not a measure of any of these traits, and because each trait implies a different therapeutic target.

evidence.snippet: BACKGROUND: Obstructive sleep apnea syndrome (OSAS), affecting approximately 1 billion adults globally, is characterized by recurrent airway obstruction during sleep, leading to oxygen desaturation, elevated carbon dioxide levels, and disrupted sleep architecture.
evidence.explanation: Defines the fundamental pathophysiological mechanism of OSA as recurrent airway obstruction during sleep.

evidence.snippet: Obstructive sleep apnea syndrome (OSAS) is characterized by intermittent hypoxia (IH) during sleep due to recurrent upper airway obstruction.
evidence.explanation: Confirms that intermittent hypoxia results from recurrent upper airway obstruction, the primary mechanical defect in OSA.

steps/1.description: During sleep the wakefulness-dependent tonic drive to the pharyngeal dilator muscles is withdrawn, and where the underlying airway is anatomically narrow or collapsible the soft tissues occlude, obstructing airflow against continued respiratory effort. Anatomical factors (retrognathia, adenotonsillar hypertrophy, obesity and parapharyngeal fat) set the collapsibility, but they are not the whole mechanism: whether an individual obstruction becomes a self-limited event or the start of a cycling pattern depends on the non-anatomic endotypic traits curated in the node below.

evidence.snippet: Obstructive sleep apnea syndrome (OSAS), affecting approximately 1 billion adults globally, is characterized by recurrent airway obstruction during sleep, leading to oxygen desaturation, elevated carbon dioxide levels, and disrupted sleep architecture.
evidence.explanation: Confirms that disrupted sleep architecture is a fundamental consequence of recurrent airway obstruction in OSA.

steps/2.description: Frequent arousals to restore airway patency disrupt sleep architecture, reducing restorative sleep and causing daytime sleepiness. The arousal is simultaneously the corrective mechanism and a source of injury, which makes the arousal threshold genuinely double-edged rather than a severity marker: a low threshold is its own endotype, since patients who arouse too readily terminate events before dilator recruitment can stabilise the airway.

evidence.snippet: The cyclic pattern of intermittent hypoxia in OSAS triggers oxidative stress, contributing to cellular damage.
evidence.explanation: Directly confirms that intermittent hypoxia in OSA triggers oxidative stress and cellular damage.

evidence.snippet: IH increases oxygen free radicals (ROS) and reduces antioxidant capacities.
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates the molecular mechanism by which intermittent hypoxia produces oxidative stress through increased ROS and decreased antioxidant defenses.

evidence.snippet: IH-induced oxidative stress (increased malondialdehyde (MDA) and NADPH oxidase (NOX) and decreased superoxide dismutase), increased inflammation (tumour necrosis factor-α, NF-κB and inducible nitric oxide synthase), HIF-1 and apoptosis evaluated by terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase dUTP nick-end labelling and cleaved caspase-3.
evidence.explanation: Meta-analysis of rodent models confirming that intermittent hypoxia induces oxidative stress, inflammation, and apoptosis in the brain, establishing causal mechanisms.

steps/3.description: Repeated cycles of oxygen desaturation followed by rapid reoxygenation. The cyclical character is the mechanistically important part: it is the reoxygenation phase, ischaemia-reperfusion-like, that generates the burst of reactive oxygen species driving oxidative stress, sympathetic activation and systemic inflammation. An equivalent time-averaged desaturation delivered continuously does not reproduce the phenotype, which is why this node - and not the apnoea count - is the causal quantity for the systemic sequelae.

evidence.snippet: Tear film stability is disrupted by inflammation and lacrimal and meibomian glands dysfunction, which are caused by intermittent hypoxia and associated oxidative stress in OSA.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the mechanistic link: intermittent hypoxia and oxidative stress in OSA drive inflammation and lacrimal/meibomian gland dysfunction that destabilize the tear film.

evidence.snippet: These disruptions result in both aqueous-deficient and evaporative forms of DED.
evidence.explanation: Confirms that OSA-driven tear film disruption produces both aqueous-deficient and evaporative forms of dry eye disease.

evidence.snippet: This review highlights the multifactorial etiology of OSA-related DED, highlighting the roles of systemic and ocular inflammation, lipid metabolism dysfunction, and mechanical stress.
evidence.explanation: Supports the multifactorial mechanism, including ocular inflammation, meibomian lipid metabolism dysfunction, and mechanical stress.

steps/4.description: Intermittent hypoxia and the associated oxidative stress in OSA drive ocular surface and systemic inflammation together with lacrimal gland dysfunction (reduced aqueous tear production) and meibomian gland dysfunction (dysregulated meibum lipid secretion). The resulting tear film instability produces both aqueous-deficient and evaporative dry eye disease. Mechanical factors such as face-down sleeping positions, habitual eye rubbing, and CPAP airflow leakage or retrograde air movement further aggravate meibomian gland dysfunction and ocular surface drying.

evidence.snippet: In male rats and mice, chronic IH simulating the repeated apnea events of OSA increased TLR4 expression in the heart, liver, and hippocampus
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates in vivo upregulation of TLR4 across multiple tissues in response to chronic intermittent hypoxia.

steps/5.description: Intermittent hypoxia and hypoxia-reoxygenation cycles trigger upregulation of Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4), a pattern-recognition receptor that recognizes damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs) released by tissue injury. TLR4 upregulation in response to IH is observed across multiple tissues including the heart, liver, and central nervous system.

evidence.snippet: TLR4 requires the adaptor protein, myeloid differentiation factor 88 (MyD88), for effective signaling, leading to the rapid activation of NF-κB and subsequent inflammatory cytokine production
evidence.explanation: Establishes the mechanistic progression from TLR4 recognition through MyD88-dependent NF-κB activation to downstream inflammatory transcription.

steps/6.description: TLR4 recruits the myeloid differentiation primary response protein (MyD88) adaptor, leading to rapid activation of nuclear factor-kappa B (NF-κB). MyD88-dependent signaling is necessary and sufficient for TLR4-driven inflammatory response and transcription of pro-inflammatory cytokines.

evidence.snippet: In animal models, chronic IH exposure increases NLRP3 inflammasome expression, and NLRP3 deficiency or inhibition protects against IH-induced inflammation, oxidative stress, and apoptosis in the brain, heart, and vasculature
evidence.explanation: Functional loss-of-function evidence that NLRP3 inflammasome activation mediates IH-induced inflammatory injury.

evidence.snippet: miR-155, miR-210, and miR-144 all provide positive feedback to NLRP3 activation
evidence.explanation: Establishes the miRNA positive-feedback arm onto NLRP3. Graded OTHER because the source supports this from non-IH systems.

evidence.snippet: the silencing of these miRNAs ameliorate IH-induced inflammation, endothelial dysfunction, and tissue injury
evidence.explanation: Loss-of-function evidence that the IH-upregulated miRNAs are functionally required for the inflammatory phenotype.

steps/7.description: Intermittent hypoxia upregulates miR-155, miR-210 and miR-144, which provide positive feedback to NLRP3 activation, and raises NLRP3 inflammasome expression directly. Assembled NLRP3 activates caspase-1, which processes pro-IL-1beta and pro-IL-18 into their bioactive forms. This arm is curated as its own node rather than as prose inside systemic inflammation because it carries the strongest causal evidence in the set: NLRP3 deficiency or inhibition protects against IH-induced injury, which is an intervention result rather than an association.

evidence.snippet: In male rats, chronic IH led to the increased phosphorylation of p38, extracellular signal-regulated kinases (ERKs), and c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK) in pancreatic tissue, which were associated with pancreatic inflammation
evidence.explanation: Documents IH-induced MAPK (p38, ERK, JNK) phosphorylation as a downstream consequence of TLR4/MyD88 signaling.

steps/8.description: Downstream of TLR4/MyD88 signaling, and in parallel with rather than downstream of NF-κB, mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) family members (p38, ERK1/2, JNK) undergo phosphorylation. These phosphorylated MAPK kinases activate additional transcription factors including AP-1, amplifying the pro-inflammatory response and driving robust production of cytokines such as TNF-α, IL-6, IL-8, and IL-1β.

steps/9.description: Intermittent hypoxia activates inflammatory pathways (NF-kB), elevating circulating CRP, IL-6, TNF-alpha, IL-8, IL-1beta and MCP-1. Cyclooxygenase-1 and COX-2 are upregulated in parallel, catalysing pro-inflammatory eicosanoids, particularly prostaglandin E2, which amplifies immune cell activation. Elevated systemic inflammation contributes to endothelial dysfunction, metabolic dysfunction and atherosclerosis. Curated in parallel with sympathetic overactivation rather than downstream of it: the two limbs are additive contributors to the vascular consequences, and both are needed to account for the hypertension.

evidence.snippet: The cyclic pattern of intermittent hypoxia in OSAS triggers oxidative stress, contributing to cellular damage.

steps/10.description: Chemoreceptor sensitisation converts a nocturnal, intermittent stimulus into a tonic daytime elevation of sympathetic vasoconstrictor outflow that persists long after waking - the step that turns a sleep disorder into a cardiovascular one - leading to hypertension, arrhythmias, and cardiovascular disease.

open_questions/0.rationale: Obstructive sleep apnea has well-established pathophysiological mechanisms linking it to cardiovascular disease (intermittent hypoxia, sympathetic activation, oxidative stress, systemic inflammation). However, randomized controlled trials of PAP therapy show inconsistent results for reducing cardiovascular events and mortality, despite improvements in intermediate markers (apnea-hypopnea index, oxygen saturation, daytime sleepiness) and intermediate cardiometabolic parameters. This suggests that either (1) mechanistic pathways are disrupted by PAP in animal models but less effectively in humans, (2) intermediate-parameter improvement alone does not guarantee hard-endpoint benefit, or (3) treatment efficacy is dependent on phenotype-specific or adherence-dependent factors not yet characterized. The gap is not at the OSA pathophysiology level but at the PAP-therapy-response level: which OSA endotypes truly benefit from PAP, through which mechanism, and under which adherence/severity conditions.

open_questions/1.rationale: Obstructive sleep apnea has established pathophysiological mechanisms linking intermittent hypoxia and sleep fragmentation to systemic inflammation and oxidative stress. However, the causal contribution of OSA to multi-organ fibrotic remodeling remains undercharacterized. Clinical and experimental evidence suggests OSA may promote fibrosis in the lungs, liver, kidneys, and heart, but the mechanistic details—how intermittent hypoxia-reoxygenation initiates TGF-beta signaling, myofibroblast activation, and ECM deposition in each organ—are incompletely defined. The degree to which fibrotic remodeling is reversible with therapy (e.g., CPAP) and the relative contributions of intermittent hypoxia versus sleep fragmentation to fibrotic progression remain understudied. Furthermore, organ-specific differences in fibrotic susceptibility and the role of tissue-resident macrophages, fibroblasts, and endothelial cells in OSA-driven remodeling require clarification. The TGF-beta → myofibroblast activation → ECM-deposition chain at issue is the conserved process modeled by the `fibrotic_response` module, so this gap is also anchored there as a candidate `conforms_to` target should the organ-specific evidence mature.

steps/8.description: The enzymatic arm of OCA. Tyrosinase (TYR) is the rate-limiting enzyme, converting tyrosine to DOPA and DOPA to dopaquinone, and it requires a neutral melanosomal pH and a copper cofactor to work at all. Two further melanosomal enzymes act downstream in the same pathway: tyrosinase-related protein 1 (TYRP1), which oxidises 5,6-dihydroxyindole-2-carboxylic acid (DHICA) monomers into melanin, and dopachrome tautomerase (DCT, also called tyrosinase-related protein 2). Loss of any of the three removes a step from eumelanin synthesis, and the severity tracks how much residual activity remains: TYR null alleles give lifelong complete absence of pigment, while TYRP1 and DCT variants leave milder hypopigmentation.

evidence.snippet: Type II, IV and VI OCA are caused by mutations of ion transport proteins OCA2, SLC45A2, and SLC24A5, respectively
evidence.explanation: The gene-to-subtype assignment behind this node's gene list, from a review of melanosomal ion transport.

evidence.snippet: All data point to the dual roles of OCA2-dependent pH regulation—for both TYR trafficking and TYR activities.
evidence.explanation: Supports the two consequences this node names for OCA2 loss: inactive tyrosinase and mis-trafficked tyrosinase.

evidence.snippet: The knockdown of SLC45A2 does not affect melanosomal morphology but induces melanosomal acidification that interrupts TYR activity [37].
evidence.explanation: Supports the SLC45A2 half of the mechanism, and distinguishes it from a melanosome-structural defect.

evidence.snippet: SLC24A5 undoubtedly plays a role in melanin production, but its subcellular localization is uncertain.
evidence.explanation: Sources the caveat this node records about SLC24A5 rather than asserting a melanosomal site for it.

steps/9.description: The non-enzymatic arm of OCA. Tyrosinase works only at neutral pH, but premelanosomes are acidic; neutralisation at the stage II-to-III transition depends on the combined action of several melanosomal membrane transport proteins. OCA2 mediates a chloride-selective anion conductance and is a positive regulator of pH neutralisation; SLC45A2 is proposed to efflux protons coupled to a sugar substrate; SLC24A5 is a potassium-dependent sodium/calcium exchanger whose subcellular site is still disputed. Losing any of them leaves the melanosome acidic, so tyrosinase is inactive and, in the case of OCA2 and SLC45A2, is also mis-trafficked and retained in the ER/Golgi rather than delivered to the melanosome. The transport activities themselves remain incompletely characterised.

evidence.snippet: Together, our results reveal that OCA7 regulates pigmentation through two well-established determinants of melanosome biogenesis and function, PMEL processing, and organelle pH.
evidence.explanation: The mechanism this node asserts, established in OCA7-knockout MNT1 melanoma cells.

steps/10.description: The OCA7 route. LRMDA (formerly C10orf11) is not an enzyme or a transporter: it is recruited to the limiting membrane of the melanosome through active RAB32, where it binds the Commander assembly, and mutations causing OCA7 uncouple that RAB32-Commander binding. Loss of LRMDA disturbs melanosome maturation itself - PMEL processing and the stage I to stage II transition - and lowers melanosomal pH, so pigment output falls without any defect in the melanogenic enzymes. LRMDA localises to melanoblasts and melanocytes in human fetal tissue but was not detected in retinal pigment epithelial cells.

evidence.snippet: Oculocutaneous albinism (OCA) is a group of inherited disorders of melanin biosynthesis characterized by a generalized reduction in pigmentation of hair, skin and eyes.
evidence.explanation: Defines OCA as a disorder of melanin biosynthesis with generalized pigmentary reduction.

steps/11.description: The convergence point of the three upstream routes. Melanin is synthesized by melanocytes (skin, hair follicle) and the retinal pigment epithelium within specialized organelles called melanosomes. Whether the lesion is in a melanogenic enzyme (TYR, TYRP1, DCT), in the melanosomal ion transport that sets the pH tyrosinase needs (OCA2, SLC45A2, SLC24A5), or in melanosome biogenesis itself (LRMDA), the result is absent or reduced melanin in melanocytes and the retinal pigment epithelium. OCA1A, with complete tyrosinase deficiency, produces no melanin throughout life, whereas hypomorphic and non-TYR forms permit some pigment accumulation.

evidence.snippet: The degree of skin and hair hypopigmentation varies with the type of OCA.
evidence.explanation: Establishes that cutaneous and hair hypopigmentation varies by OCA subtype.

evidence.snippet: In the skin, melanin acts as a broadband protectant against UV light and has free radical scavenging and antioxidant properties
evidence.explanation: Explains why loss of cutaneous melanin in OCA increases vulnerability to UV-induced skin damage.

steps/12.description: Reduced or absent melanin in epidermal and hair-follicle melanocytes produces variable hypopigmentation of the skin and hair. In OCA1A there is a complete and lifelong absence of pigment (white hair and skin); in OCA1B, OCA2, OCA3, and OCA4 some pigment accumulates over time, and OCA3 in particular can present with reddish-brown (rufous) coloration. Because melanin acts as a broadband ultraviolet protectant and free-radical scavenger, its loss leaves the skin vulnerable to UV-induced damage and an increased risk of skin cancer, especially squamous cell carcinoma in sun-exposed populations.

evidence.snippet: Misrouting of the optic nerves is a characteristic finding, resulting in strabismus and reduced stereoscopic vision.

evidence.snippet: patients with albinism experience a decrease in best-corrected visual acuity and stereopsis due to developmental eye abnormalities, namely hypoplasia of the fovea

evidence.snippet: Although foveal differentiation begins around 22 weeks of gestation, it continues for months postnatally, offering a potential therapeutic window

steps/13.description: Melanin in the retinal pigment epithelium is required for normal postnatal development of the fovea and for correct routing of retinal ganglion cell axons. Reduced RPE and iris melanin in OCA leads to foveal hypoplasia, reduced visual acuity, fundus hypopigmentation, and iris transillumination. Crucially, a melanin defect in the RPE causes abnormal decussation (misrouting) of retinal ganglion cell axons at the optic chiasm, with an excess of fibers crossing to the contralateral side; this produces reduced stereoscopic vision and contributes to strabismus. The precise mechanism by which an RPE pigment defect disrupts development of the adjacent neural retina remains incompletely understood, but foveal differentiation continues for months after birth, offering a potential therapeutic window.

steps/1.description: FKBP10 encodes FKBP65, a 65 kDa endoplasmic-reticulum-resident peptidyl-prolyl cis-trans isomerase and immunophilin that acts as a chaperone in type I procollagen folding and maturation. Biallelic loss-of-function FKBP10 variants (frameshifts and premature termination codons causing mRNA instability, or missense variants causing loss of most of the protein) eliminate FKBP65 from the ER. In contrast to the prolyl 3-hydroxylation complex (CRTAP/P3H1/CyPB, deficient in OI types VII/VIII/IX), loss of FKBP65 leaves general collagen helical folding, chain incorporation and thermal stability largely intact, pointing to a more specialized role in collagen post-translational modification rather than bulk folding.

evidence.snippet: there is diminished hydroxylation of the telopeptide lysyl residues involved in intermolecular cross-link formation in bone. The phenotype overlaps with that seen with mutations in PLOD2 (Bruck syndrome II), which encodes LH2, the enzyme that hydroxylates the telopeptide lysyl residues.
evidence.explanation: Documents diminished telopeptide lysyl hydroxylation and intermolecular cross-linking on FKBP65 loss, and the mechanistic overlap with PLOD2/LH2 Bruck syndrome type II.

evidence.snippet: Mass spectrometry reveals absence of hydroxylation of the collagen telopeptide lysine involved in cross-linking, suggesting that FKBP65 is required for lysyl hydroxylase activity or access to type I collagen telopeptide lysines, perhaps through its function as a peptidylprolyl isomerase.
evidence.explanation: Provides direct mass-spectrometry evidence that FKBP65 loss abolishes telopeptide lysine hydroxylation, the cross-linking defect underlying the matrix abnormality.

steps/2.description: FKBP65 is required for hydroxylation of the telopeptide lysyl residues that form the intermolecular cross-links of bone collagen, acting through or alongside the lysyl hydroxylase LH2 (PLOD2) — possibly via its peptidyl-prolyl isomerase function granting LH2 access to the telopeptide lysines. In its absence, mass spectrometry shows near-absence of telopeptide lysine hydroxylation in secreted collagen, producing diminished intermolecular cross-linking. This shared telopeptide-cross-linking axis mechanistically links FKBP10-related OI to PLOD2-related Bruck syndrome type II.

evidence.snippet: there is a dramatic decrease in collagen deposited in culture despite normal collagen secretion.
evidence.explanation: Documents the reduced extracellular-matrix collagen deposition that produces the defective bone matrix in OI type XI.

evidence.snippet: Immunofluorescence shows sparse, disorganized collagen fibrils in proband matrix.
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates the sparse, disorganized collagen fibril architecture of the defective bone matrix underlying fragility.

steps/3.description: The undercrosslinked collagen is deposited into the extracellular matrix in markedly reduced amounts despite near-normal secretion, producing sparse, disorganized collagen fibrils and a collagen-to-mineral matrix ratio far below normal. The structurally inadequate, abnormally mineralized bone matrix yields low bone mass and severe skeletal fragility, manifesting clinically as recurrent fractures, bone deformity, progressive scoliosis and short stature; in the Bruck-overlap arm of the spectrum, congenital joint contractures accompany the bone fragility.

edges/1.description: Without FKBP65, hydroxylation of the collagen telopeptide lysines required for intermolecular cross-link formation is diminished, reducing collagen cross-linking.

edges/2.description: Undercrosslinked collagen is poorly deposited into the extracellular matrix, forming a sparse, disorganized, abnormally mineralized bone matrix that is mechanically fragile.

evidence.snippet: homozygosity for mutations in FKBP10, which encodes FKBP65, a chaperone that participates in type I procollagen folding, was identified. Further, we determined that FKBP10 mutations affect type I procollagen secretion.

evidence.snippet: Here we describe five families with OI-like bone fragility in association with congenital contractures who all had FKBP10 mutations. Therefore, we conclude that FKBP10 mutations are a cause of recessive osteogenesis imperfecta and Bruck syndrome

genes/0.notes: OI type XI is caused by biallelic loss-of-function variants in FKBP10, which encodes the 65 kDa ER peptidyl-prolyl cis-trans isomerase/chaperone FKBP65. The same gene underlies both contracture-free recessive OI and Bruck-syndrome-like OI with congenital contractures (FKBP10-related Bruck syndrome, often designated Bruck syndrome type 1), reflecting a phenotypic continuum.

evidence.snippet: Bisphosphonates continue to be used most extensively in those with vertebral fractures, frequent long bone fractures, or more severe OI.

evidence.explanation: GeneReviews documents intramedullary rodding as standard orthopedic management for OI long-bone fractures and deformity.

treatments/2.description: Physical and occupational therapy increase mobility and muscle strength, improve bone stability, and help prevent contractures and deformity — of particular relevance in the Bruck-overlap arm with congenital joint contractures; early physical therapy follows brief post-fracture immobilization.

evidence.snippet: proalpha1(I) cleavage was not enhanced by an excess of the mutant protein, proving that the Phe249Leu mutation leads to a BMP1/mTLD protein with deficient PICP proteolytic activity.

evidence.snippet: we found a homozygous causative BMP1 mutation, c.34G>C, in a consanguineous family affected by increased bone mineral density and multiple recurrent fractures.
evidence.explanation: Identifies a homozygous BMP1 mutation underlying bone fragility with increased bone mineral density, defining the disorder.

steps/1.description: BMP1 encodes the secreted astacin metalloprotease bone morphogenetic protein 1 and its longer isoform mammalian Tolloid (mTLD), which together constitute the principal procollagen C-terminal-propeptide (PICP) endopeptidase for type I procollagen. Biallelic loss-of-function BMP1 variants (e.g., the protease-domain p.Phe249Leu missense and signal-peptide variants) destroy or attenuate this proteolytic activity, so excess mutant BMP1/mTLD fails to enhance cleavage of the C-terminal propeptide of proalpha1(I). This is a proteolytic (enzymatic) lesion, mechanistically distinct from the chaperone and prolyl-3-hydroxylation defects of other recessive OI types.

evidence.snippet: BMP1/mTLD-deficiency in humans not only results in delayed cleavage of the type I procollagen C-propeptide but also hampers the processing of the small leucine-rich proteoglycan prodecorin, a regulator of collagen fibrillogenesis.
evidence.explanation: Documents the dual procollagen C-propeptide and prodecorin processing defect that disrupts collagen fibrillogenesis in BMP1-related OI.

evidence.snippet: transmission electron microscopy of the dermis show impaired assembly of heterotypic type I/V collagen fibrils in the ECM.
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates impaired heterotypic collagen fibril assembly resulting from BMP1/mTLD deficiency.

steps/2.description: Deficient BMP1/mTLD activity causes delayed cleavage of the type I procollagen C-propeptide and also hampers processing of prodecorin, a small leucine-rich proteoglycan that regulates collagen fibrillogenesis. The combined defect impairs assembly of mature heterotypic type I/V collagen fibrils in the extracellular matrix, yielding a structurally abnormal bone collagen scaffold.

evidence.snippet: It thus appears that disturbed C-propeptide cleavage impairs mineralization in two ways: first, the onset of mineralization is delayed, leading to an increased amount of unmineralized osteoid, and second, once mineralization starts, too much mineral is incorporated into the bone matrix, resulting in hypermineralization.
evidence.explanation: Documents the dual mineralization defect (hyperosteoidosis plus hypermineralization) of the bone matrix in BMP1-related OI.

evidence.snippet: Bmp1a is critically required for mature-collagen generation, downstream of osteoblast maturation, in bone.
evidence.explanation: Zebrafish bmp1a data establish that BMP1 is required downstream of osteoblast maturation for mature collagen generation in bone, underlying the matrix fragility.

steps/3.description: The abnormal collagen matrix in BMP1/mTLD deficiency mineralizes aberrantly: histomorphometry shows hyperosteoidosis with delayed onset of mineralization, yet the mineralized matrix becomes hypermineralized (high calcium content). The net result is bone that is paradoxically dense (high areal bone mineral density) but mechanically brittle, producing recurrent fractures, deformity, and short stature. This high-bone-mass fragility distinguishes OI type XIII from the typically low-density recessive OI types.

edges/1.description: Without BMP1/mTLD C-proteinase activity, the type I procollagen C-propeptide is not cleaved normally, impairing maturation and assembly of collagen fibrils.

edges/2.description: The defective collagen scaffold yields an abnormally mineralized bone matrix that, despite high mineral content, is mechanically weak and fracture-prone.

evidence.snippet: Surveillance: To detect tumors at the earliest, most treatable stages: Children (age <18 years). Yearly thyroid ultrasound from the time of diagnosis (earliest reported at age 7 years) and skin check with physical examination. Adults. Yearly thyroid ultrasound and dermatologic evaluation. Women beginning at age 30 years. Monthly breast self-examination; annual breast screening (at minimum mammogram; MRI may also be incorporated). Starting by age 35 years, consider transvaginal ultrasound or endometrial biopsy. Men and women. Colonoscopy beginning at age 35 years with frequency dependent on degree of polyposis identified or family history of early-onset colon cancer (before age 40); biennial (every 2 years) renal imaging (CT or MRI preferred) beginning at age 40 years.
