evidence.explanation: Confirms hypertension as a presenting symptom in Wilms tumor patients. As for hematuria above, the snippet's 35% is an upper bound over the union of four symptoms and states no rate for hypertension alone, so the band is OCCASIONAL (5-29%) rather than FREQUENT (30-79%).

steps/26.description: Hypertension occurs in patients with Wilms tumor due to renin secretion by the tumor or renal artery compression.

evidence.snippet: However, up to 35% of patients can present with either hematuria, hypertension, fever, or flank pain
evidence.explanation: Lists fever among presenting symptoms in Wilms tumor patients.

steps/27.description: Low-grade fever may occur as a constitutional symptom.

evidence.snippet: However, up to 35% of patients can present with either hematuria, hypertension, fever, or flank pain
evidence.explanation: Confirms flank pain as one of the presenting symptoms of Wilms tumor.

steps/28.description: Flank pain may be a presenting symptom, and rarely, patients present with acute abdomen in the setting of tumor rupture.

edges/11.description: WT1 loss prevents normal renal blastemal differentiation

edges/12.description: Loss of WTX stabilizes beta-catenin signaling in nephrogenic progenitors

edges/13.description: Exon 3 mutations stabilize beta-catenin and drive constitutive Wnt output

edges/14.description: Constitutive beta-catenin signaling prevents normal nephron maturation

edges/15.description: Wnt output maintains embryonal renal progenitors in a self-renewing compartment

edges/16.description: Developmental arrest preserves proliferative embryonal renal cells

edges/17.description: Biallelic IGF2 expression expands fetal renal progenitors

edges/18.description: miRNA dysregulation reinforces the undifferentiated proliferative compartment

edges/19.description: SIX1/SIX2-mutant progenitors retain a proliferative embryonal identity

edges/20.description: Loss of REST repression is proposed to act on the same developmental arrest that the other Wilms tumor suppressor lesions converge on; the intervening steps between reduced REST repression and persistence of nephrogenic rests are not established.

evidence.snippet: The tumors were bilateral in six patients, and 10/11 tumors are accompanied by perilobar nephrogenic rests.
evidence.explanation: Reports the perilobar nephrogenic rests and the bilaterality that this edge is drawn from.

edges/21.description: Kidneys resected from children with germline TRIM28 loss usually carry perilobar nephrogenic rests, the persisting embryonal remnants this node describes; the steps from TRIM28 loss to rest persistence are not established.

edges/22.description: Persisting blastemal clones expand into overt nephroblastoma

edges/23.description: Acquisition of TP53 dysfunction drives aggressive anaplastic evolution in a subset of tumors

edges/24.description: An expanding intrarenal mass is what a parent or clinician palpates, which is the usual route to diagnosis.

edges/25.description: Tumor invasion of the collecting system releases blood into the urine.

edges/26.description: Raised blood pressure is one of the presenting features of the renal tumor.

edges/27.description: Flank pain follows capsular stretch, and acute abdominal pain follows tumor rupture.

edges/28.description: Fever occurs as a constitutional accompaniment of the tumor rather than through an established mechanism.

evidence.snippet: In 1990, mutations of the Wilms' tumor-1 gene (WT1), encoding a transcription factor in the embryonic kidney, were found in 10-15% of Wilms' tumors; germline WT1 mutations were associated with hereditary syndromes involving glomerular and reproductive tract dysplasia.
evidence.explanation: Confirms WT1 mutation frequency and germline association with hereditary syndromes.

genes/0.notes: WT1 mutations occur in 10-15% of sporadic Wilms tumors. Germline WT1 mutations cause predisposition syndromes (WAGR, Denys-Drash, Frasier). WT1 is a transcription factor essential for kidney development.

evidence.snippet: This has been illustrated by the findings that mutations of Wnt/β-catenin pathway-related WT1, β-catenin, and WTX together account for about one-third of Wilms tumor cases.
evidence.explanation: Confirms CTNNB1 as one of the key mutated genes in Wilms tumor contributing to Wnt pathway activation.

genes/1.notes: Activating mutations in CTNNB1 (beta-catenin) occur in approximately 15% of Wilms tumors, leading to constitutive Wnt pathway activation.

evidence.snippet: This has been illustrated by the findings that mutations of Wnt/β-catenin pathway-related WT1, β-catenin, and WTX together account for about one-third of Wilms tumor cases.
evidence.explanation: Confirms WTX (AMER1) as one of the key mutated genes in Wilms tumor.

genes/2.notes: WTX inactivation occurs in 15-20% of Wilms tumors. WTX negatively regulates Wnt signaling, and its loss leads to pathway activation.

evidence.snippet: epigenetic changes, particularly the loss of imprinting of the DNA region encoding the major fetal growth factor IGF2, which results in its biallelic over-expression, are closely associated with the development of many Wilms tumors.
evidence.explanation: Confirms loss of imprinting at IGF2/11p15 locus in Wilms tumor development.

genes/3.notes: Loss of imprinting at 11p15, leading to biallelic IGF2 expression, occurs in approximately 70% of Wilms tumors. This is also the mechanism in Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome.

evidence.snippet: gain of chromosome 1q is one of the most commonly observed cytogenetic abnormalities in WT, seen in as many as 30% of patients
evidence.explanation: Confirms 1q gain frequency and its status as a common cytogenetic abnormality in Wilms tumor.

evidence.snippet: A retrospective analysis of more than 1000 patients in NWTS-5 demonstrated that 1q gain was associated with inferior EFS and OS across all tumor stages
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates prognostic significance of 1q gain across all stages.

genes/4.notes: Gain of chromosome 1q is one of the most commonly observed cytogenetic abnormalities in Wilms tumor, seen in approximately 30% of patients. It is associated with inferior event-free survival and overall survival across all tumor stages.

evidence.snippet: Combined LOH 1p and 16q has limited impact as a prognostic marker because only 5% of favorable histology WT carry this molecular change.
evidence.explanation: Supports the ~5% frequency in favorable-histology Wilms tumor and, explicitly, the limited practical impact of this marker — the source qualifies rather than confirms its prognostic utility.

genes/5.notes: Loss of heterozygosity at both chromosome 1p and 16q identifies a favorable-histology subgroup with increased relapse risk, and COG protocols augment therapy on this basis. Its practical value as a stratification marker is nevertheless limited because only about 5% of favorable-histology Wilms tumors carry the combined change, so it reclassifies few patients. Chromosome 1q gain has largely superseded it as the more informative copy-number marker.

evidence.snippet: careful analysis including copy number assessment and immunohistochemistry, as well as confirming that anaplasia was present in the portion of tumor undergoing mutation analysis, indicated that nearly all anaplastic WT have TP53 mutations if one looks hard enough
evidence.explanation: Confirms near-universal TP53 mutation in anaplastic Wilms tumors when thoroughly assessed.

genes/6.notes: Nearly all diffuse anaplastic Wilms tumors harbor TP53 mutations when adequately assayed — earlier series reporting roughly 50-60% understated the true rate because they did not combine copy-number assessment and immunohistochemistry, or did not confirm that the tumor portion undergoing mutation analysis actually contained anaplasia. TP53 dysfunction drives anaplastic transformation and is associated with poor prognosis and therapy resistance.

evidence.snippet: Recurrent mutations included a hotspot mutation (Q177R) in the homeo-domain of SIX1 and SIX2 in tumors with high proliferative potential (18.1% of blastemal cases); mutations in the DROSHA/DGCR8 microprocessor genes (18.2% of blastemal cases)
evidence.explanation: Establishes DROSHA as a recurrent somatic lesion of the tumor, found by exome sequencing of blastemal-type Wilms tumors at a rate comparable to the SIX1/SIX2 hotspot in the same series. This is the basis for typing the record SOMATIC_DRIVER rather than a germline predisposition locus.

evidence.snippet: Recent investigations also revealed that mutations of Drosha and Dicer, the RNases required for miRNA generation, and Dis3L2, the 3'-5' exonuclease that normally degrades miRNAs and mRNAs, could cause predisposition to Wilms tumors, demonstrating that miRNA can play a pivotal role in Wilms tumor development.
evidence.explanation: Confirms mutations in miRNA processing enzymes as a mechanism of Wilms tumor predisposition.

genes/7.notes: In Wilms tumor DROSHA is mutated in the tumor itself: exome and transcriptome sequencing of blastemal-type tumors found DROSHA/DGCR8 microprocessor mutations in 18.2 per cent of blastemal cases, beside the SIX1/SIX2 hotspot, which is why this record is typed as a somatic driver. The predisposition wording in the PMID:25018051 sentence this record also cites applies to DICER1 and DIS3L2 (the 3'-5' exonuclease that degrades miRNAs and mRNAs, mutated in Perlman syndrome), whose germline lesions are the predisposition alleles of this group. Loss of miRNA processing is thought to derepress target genes controlling nephron progenitor differentiation; the let-7/LIN28 axis is the most commonly proposed effector, but that specific mechanism is not covered by the evidence cited here and is recorded as context rather than a curated claim.

evidence.snippet: Recent investigations also revealed that mutations of Drosha and Dicer, the RNases required for miRNA generation, and Dis3L2, the 3'-5' exonuclease that normally degrades miRNAs and mRNAs, could cause predisposition to Wilms tumors, demonstrating that miRNA can play a pivotal role in Wilms tumor development.
evidence.explanation: Confirms mutations in miRNA processing enzymes as a mechanism of Wilms tumor predisposition.

evidence.snippet: Nevertheless, WT also occurs in the context of more pleiotropic cancer predispositions, such as DICER1, Li-Fraumeni and Bloom syndrome, as well as Fanconi anemia.
evidence.explanation: Places germline DICER1 among the pleiotropic cancer predispositions in which Wilms tumor occurs, which is why the syndrome itself is a separate entry.

genes/8.notes: DICER1 is the other of the two RNases required for miRNA generation named in the cited series. Germline DICER1 variants cause a pleiotropic tumor predisposition condition of which Wilms tumor is one manifestation; that condition is curated as its own entry, DICER1_Tumor_Predisposition_Syndrome, and this record covers only the Wilms tumor relationship.

evidence.snippet: Recurrent mutations included a hotspot mutation (Q177R) in the homeo-domain of SIX1 and SIX2 in tumors with high proliferative potential (18.1% of blastemal cases)
evidence.explanation: Landmark genomic study directly demonstrating recurrent SIX1/SIX2 Q177R mutations in 18.1% of blastemal-type Wilms tumors.

genes/9.notes: Recurrent SIX1/SIX2 Q177R homeodomain mutations occur in 18.1% of blastemal-type Wilms tumors. These mutations are associated with high proliferative potential and chemotherapy-resistant blastemal tumors. The cited series reports the Q177R hotspot in both paralogs.

evidence.snippet: Recurrent mutations included a hotspot mutation (Q177R) in the homeo-domain of SIX1 and SIX2 in tumors with high proliferative potential (18.1% of blastemal cases)
evidence.explanation: Landmark genomic study directly demonstrating recurrent SIX1/SIX2 Q177R mutations in 18.1% of blastemal-type Wilms tumors.

genes/10.notes: The Q177R homeodomain hotspot reported for SIX1 is reported in the same series for its paralog SIX2.

evidence.snippet: Here we describe 11 different inactivating mutations in the REST gene (encoding RE1-silencing transcription factor) in four familial Wilms tumor pedigrees and nine non-familial cases.
evidence.explanation: Establishes REST as a Wilms tumor predisposition gene with an inactivating lesion class.

evidence.snippet: We identified a second mutational event in two tumors, suggesting that REST may act as a tumor-suppressor gene in Wilms tumor pathogenesis.
evidence.explanation: Supports a tumor suppressor reading rather than a purely constitutional risk allele.

genes/11.notes: A constitutional REST lesion is a Wilms tumor predisposition condition in its own right; MONDO carries it as Wilms tumor 6 (MONDO:0014779) under hereditary Wilms tumor, and that condition belongs in its own entry. What is recorded here is the gene's behaviour inside the tumor, which the REST Repressor Inactivation node models.

evidence.snippet: We also found a strong association with the rare epithelial subtype of Wilms tumour, with 14 of 16 tumours being epithelial or epithelial predominant.
evidence.explanation: Records the association with epithelial histology, which is the feature that selects patients for TRIM28 testing.

evidence.snippet: Exome sequencing on eight tumor DNA samples from six individuals showed loss-of-heterozygosity (LOH) of the TRIM28-locus by mitotic recombination in seven tumors, suggesting that TRIM28 functions as a tumor suppressor gene in Wilms tumor development.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the constitutional variant plus somatic loss of the wild type allele as the mechanism.

genes/12.notes: Every inherited variant reported in the largest exome series was maternally transmitted. The associated tumor is characteristically epithelial or epithelial predominant, which is the histological clue to testing. MONDO carries the condition as Wilms tumor 7 (MONDO:0979876) under hereditary Wilms tumor, and that condition is curated as its own entry, TRIM28-Related_Wilms_Tumor_Predisposition; the tumor side of the mechanism is the TRIM28 Tumor Suppressor Loss node.

evidence.snippet: The COG approach of upfront nephrectomy allows for immediate histologic diagnosis, molecular analysis, and accurate local staging assessment.
evidence.explanation: Confirms the role of nephrectomy as primary surgical approach in COG trials.

evidence.snippet: Advances in multimodal therapy including surgery, chemotherapy, and radiation therapy given according to risk stratification have allowed most patients to achieve survival rates in excess of 90%.
evidence.explanation: Confirms the multimodal approach including surgery achieves >90% survival.

treatments/0.description: Nephrectomy is the primary treatment for unilateral Wilms tumor. In North America (COG), upfront nephrectomy provides staging information and allows for immediate histologic diagnosis and molecular analysis. In Europe (SIOP), preoperative chemotherapy is given first. Both approaches achieve similar survival rates.

evidence.snippet: Advances in multimodal therapy including surgery, chemotherapy, and radiation therapy given according to risk stratification have allowed most patients to achieve survival rates in excess of 90%.
evidence.explanation: Establishes surgery as a core component of curative multimodal therapy that removes the primary tumor and contributes to >90% survival, supporting nephrectomy's action on the tumor-outgrowth node.

treatments/0/targets/0.description: Nephrectomy physically removes the primary tumor mass, eliminating the bulk of the malignant nephron progenitor-derived outgrowth.

evidence.snippet: The most common drugs used were vincristine and actinomycin D (78%). Only 12 patients (28%) received anthracyclines.
evidence.explanation: Confirms vincristine and dactinomycin as backbone chemotherapy with anthracyclines reserved for higher-risk patients.

evidence.snippet: Stepwise advances made by the National Wilms Tumor Study Group (NWTSG), which was succeeded by the Children's Oncology Group (COG), and the International Society of Pediatric Oncology (SIOP) Renal Tumor Study Group (RTSG) have not only improved survival to 90%, but have also decreased the burden of therapy
evidence.explanation: Confirms that stepwise refinement of chemotherapy has improved survival to 90%.

treatments/1.description: Actinomycin D and vincristine form the backbone of treatment for favorable histology tumors. Doxorubicin and other agents are added for higher-stage or anaplastic tumors. Cyclophosphamide and etoposide are added for the highest-risk patients.

evidence.snippet: Blastemal-type Wilms tumour (BT-WT) has been identified as a high risk histological subgroup in WT assessed after pre-nephrectomy chemotherapy in trials of the International Society of Paediatric Oncology (SIOP) Renal Tumour Study Group. Therefore, in SIOPWT2001, post-operative chemotherapy for BT-WT was intensified aiming to improve survival.
evidence.explanation: The SIOP-RTSG report shows that the chemoresistant blastemal progenitor state is specifically targeted by intensified post-operative chemotherapy, the mechanism this treatment addresses.

treatments/1/targets/0.description: Blastemal-predominant histology persisting after preoperative chemotherapy marks a chemoresistant, high-risk primitive progenitor state; it is targeted with intensified post-operative chemotherapy regimens (adding doxorubicin and, for higher stages, etoposide, cyclophosphamide, and carboplatin) to reduce relapse risk.

evidence.snippet: have not only improved survival to 90%, but have also decreased the burden of therapy
evidence.explanation: Documents that successive cooperative-group chemotherapy refinements improved survival to 90%, supporting chemotherapy's action on the tumor-outgrowth node.

treatments/1/targets/1.description: Cytotoxic chemotherapy eliminates residual and metastatic tumor cells, reducing gross tumor burden and preventing local and systemic recurrence.

evidence.snippet: The objectives for the treatment of Wilms tumor in both the Children's Oncology Group (COG) and the International Society of Paediatric Oncology (SIOP) have focused on improving cure rates and minimizing toxicity by limiting the use of radiation and doxorubicin.
evidence.explanation: Confirms radiation therapy is part of standard treatment while efforts focus on minimizing its use to reduce toxicity.

treatments/2.description: Flank radiation is used for stage III tumors and higher. Whole abdominal radiation is used for tumor rupture or diffuse peritoneal contamination. Whole lung irradiation is used for pulmonary metastases that fail to respond completely to chemotherapy.

evidence.snippet: focused on improving cure rates and minimizing toxicity by limiting the use of radiation and doxorubicin
evidence.explanation: Confirms radiation therapy as an established local-control modality for Wilms tumor burden, used in a risk-adapted manner to preserve cure rates.

treatments/2/targets/0.description: Ionizing radiation induces DNA double-strand breaks in tumor cells, eliminating residual local and metastatic Wilms tumor burden not controlled by surgery or chemotherapy.

evidence.snippet: The purpose of this study is to find out whether selinexor is an effective treatment for people who have a relapsed/refractory Wilms tumor, rhabdoid tumor, MPNST, BCOR-driven sarcoma, or another solid tumor that makes a higher than normal amount of XPO1 or has genetic changes that increase the activity of XP01.
evidence.explanation: Supports selinexor as an investigational Wilms tumor therapy through an active Wilms-specific cohort in a pediatric solid tumor trial.

treatments/3.description: Selinexor is an oral XPO1 inhibitor under clinical evaluation for recurrent or refractory Wilms tumor and other pediatric solid tumors.

evidence.snippet: The purpose of this study is to find out whether selinexor is an effective treatment for people who have a relapsed/refractory Wilms tumor, rhabdoid tumor, MPNST, BCOR-driven sarcoma, or another solid tumor that makes a higher than normal amount of XPO1
evidence.explanation: The trial evaluates selinexor (an XPO1 inhibitor) against relapsed/ refractory Wilms tumor overexpressing XPO1, supporting its action on the tumor-outgrowth node.

treatments/3/targets/0.description: Selinexor blocks XPO1-mediated nuclear export, forcing nuclear accumulation of tumor suppressors (TP53, FOXO, RB) that restrict Wilms tumor cell proliferation and survival.

evidence.snippet: Pristanic acid levels were highly elevated and dietary modification was recommended.
evidence.explanation: Human clinical basis for treating dietary intake as a modifiable factor in this disease.

evidence.snippet: This enzyme is responsible for the conversion of pristanoyl-CoA and C27-bile acyl-CoAs to their (S)-stereoisomers, which are the only stereoisomers that can be degraded via peroxisomal beta-oxidation.
evidence.explanation: States the enzymatic function and, critically, the stereospecificity of the downstream pathway - the reason loss of a racemase is a hard block rather than a slowdown.

steps/2.description: Biallelic AMACR variants abolish alpha-methylacyl-CoA racemase activity. The enzyme interconverts the (R)- and (S)-stereoisomers at the 2-methyl (or 25-methyl) position of branched-chain acyl-CoA esters. Peroxisomal beta-oxidation is stereospecific and accepts only the (S)-form, so the racemase is an obligatory gate rather than an accessory step - which is why a single enzyme loss blocks two unrelated substrate streams.

evidence.snippet: α-Methylacyl-CoA racemase (Amacr) catalyzes the racemization of the 25-methyl group in C27-intermediates in bile acid synthesis and in methyl-branched fatty acids such as pristanic acid, a metabolite derived from phytol.
evidence.explanation: States both substrate streams explicitly. Graded OTHER because this is the paper's background statement of enzymology rather than a result of its mouse experiments.

steps/3.description: With no (S)-stereoisomer available, peroxisomal beta-oxidation of 2-methyl-branched substrates stops. The block is upstream of two independent downstream streams that share nothing but this enzyme.

evidence.snippet: We describe here three patients with elevated plasma concentrations of pristanic acid (a branched-chain fatty acid) and C27-bile-acid intermediates.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the accumulating metabolites in the original patients.

evidence.snippet: patients with Amacr deficiency accumulate C27-bile acid intermediates, pristanic and phytanic acid and display sensorimotor neuropathy, seizures and relapsing encephalopathy
evidence.explanation: Links the accumulating metabolites to the neurological phenotype.

steps/4.description: Pristanic acid accumulates, with phytanic acid alongside it. Both derive from dietary phytol, so this arm of the disease is the one with an exogenous input - which is what makes dietary restriction plausible as therapy and what the mouse model demonstrates most sharply.

evidence.snippet: In 5/9 adult patients, retinitis pigmentosa was detected at a median age of 45 years (range 30-61).
evidence.explanation: Establishes the retinal lesion and its frequency in the adult cohort.

evidence.snippet: One patient also had pigmentary retinopathy, suggesting Refsum disease
evidence.explanation: Graded INDIRECT: it evidences the retinopathy and the Refsum parallel that motivates placing this node downstream of phytanic acid accumulation, without demonstrating the mechanism in AMACR deficiency.

steps/5.description: The retinal arm, which the natural-history cohort makes the leading adult presentation: retinitis pigmentosa in 5 of 9 adults, at a median age of 45, typically decades before the neurological features. Modelled downstream of the phytanic/pristanic accumulation because the same accumulation causes retinopathy in Refsum disease - but the mechanism has not been demonstrated in AMACR deficiency specifically, hence the unknown intermediates.

evidence.snippet: Two of the patients suffered from adult-onset sensory motor neuropathy. One patient also had pigmentary retinopathy, suggesting Refsum disease, whereas the other patient had upper motor neuron signs in the legs, suggesting adrenomyeloneuropathy.
evidence.explanation: The original clinical description, including both mimicked diagnoses.

steps/6.description: The tissue-level lesion behind the classic adult presentation. It is a diagnostic mimic: of the first two adult patients, one had pigmentary retinopathy suggesting Refsum disease and the other upper motor neuron signs suggesting adrenomyeloneuropathy - and both of those differentials are themselves disorders of branched-chain fatty acid handling, so the confusion is mechanistically principled rather than superficial.

evidence.snippet: Elevated C27-bile acid intermediates, C29-dicarboxylic acid, and pristanic acid were observed in all AMACR patients.
evidence.explanation: Documents the accumulating species in every AMACR patient in a prospective treatment cohort, including the C29-dicarboxylic acid.

steps/7.description: DHCA and THCA, the C27 precursors of the mature C24 bile acids, cannot be shortened and accumulate, along with a C29-dicarboxylic acid. The accumulating intermediates are hepatotoxic and mature bile acid synthesis is deficient, which is the basis both for the liver phenotype and for treating with cholic acid.

evidence.snippet: Since its first report in 2000, several children were diagnosed via molecular analyses, mostly due to elevated liver enzymes.
evidence.explanation: Establishes raised liver enzymes as the usual route to diagnosis in childhood.

steps/8.description: The childhood presentation. Persistently elevated liver enzymes, with or without cholestatic jaundice, and coagulopathy - which in a child is the combination the review argues should trigger measurement of peroxisomal metabolites. Some children are otherwise entirely asymptomatic and come to attention only through incidental blood tests.

evidence.snippet: there is a risk of liver fibrosis/cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma in these patients, requiring active monitoring
evidence.explanation: Establishes the fibrosis-cirrhosis-HCC sequence and the surveillance conclusion drawn from it.

steps/9.description: Chronic hepatic injury progressing to fibrosis and cirrhosis, and the substrate on which hepatocellular carcinoma arises. The cohort authors treat this as a surveillance obligation rather than an incidental association, which is why it is modelled as its own node rather than folded into the acute hepatic injury above it.

evidence.snippet: A female in her seventh decade presented with episodes of dysphasia, headache and sensory disturbance inconsistent with migraine, epilepsy or transient ischaemic attack.
evidence.explanation: Describes the stroke-like episodes and the differentials they defeat.

evidence.snippet: After eight years of symptoms, she developed a febrile encephalopathy with hemispheric dysfunction, focal convulsive seizures and coma.
evidence.explanation: Documents the severe end of the episodic phenotype and the length of the diagnostic delay.

steps/10.description: Episodic neurological decompensation - dysphasia, headache, sensory disturbance - that resembles neither migraine nor epilepsy nor TIA, and which in the oldest reported patient was investigated for mitochondrial disease for eight years before whole genome sequencing gave the answer. Escalation to febrile encephalopathy with coma is described.

evidence.snippet: several children were diagnosed via molecular analyses, mostly due to elevated liver enzymes
evidence.explanation: Names raised liver enzymes as the predominant presenting abnormality in childhood.

steps/11.description: Persistently raised liver enzymes, the commonest route to diagnosis in childhood and sometimes the only abnormality.

evidence.snippet: in every children with persistently elevated liver enzymes, especially with coagulopathy and with or without cholestatic jaundice
evidence.explanation: Names cholestatic jaundice in the presenting picture while marking it optional, which is why the frequency is OCCASIONAL rather than FREQUENT.

steps/12.description: Cholestatic jaundice in the childhood presentation. Explicitly qualified as "with or without" in the review's diagnostic recommendation, so it is not obligate.

evidence.snippet: especially with coagulopathy and with or without cholestatic jaundice
evidence.explanation: Names coagulopathy as a suspicion-raising feature of the childhood presentation.

steps/13.description: Coagulopathy, reflecting impaired fat-soluble vitamin K absorption from deficient mature bile acid synthesis. Singled out by the review as the feature that should raise suspicion alongside raised transaminases.

evidence.snippet: One patient was diagnosed with liver fibrosis (patient 3), while all patients underwent regular abdominal ultrasounds and in most cases FibroScan
evidence.explanation: Gives both the count and the ascertainment method, which is what makes 1/12 a screened rate rather than a clinical one.

evidence.snippet: none of them had a history of cholestasis or showed any signs of clinically evident liver disease or fibrosis
evidence.explanation: The paediatric negative. Records that the three children were fibrosis-free despite elevated transaminases, which is the age dependence this phenotype's description states.

steps/14.description: Liver fibrosis in 1 of 12 cohort patients, under a surveillance programme in which all patients had regular abdominal ultrasound and most had FibroScan - so this is a screened rate rather than a clinically apparent one. None of the three children showed fibrosis, consistent with it being a consequence of chronic rather than acute hepatic injury. Cirrhosis is modelled at the mechanism node but is deliberately not curated as a phenotype: the cohort reports the fibrosis-cirrhosis-HCC risk as a surveillance rationale, and no cohort patient is reported as cirrhotic.

evidence.snippet: Two patients had a history of cholecystectomy due to gallstones (patient 4 and 6, respectively around age 40 and 15 years).
evidence.explanation: Gives the count and both ages, including the juvenile case.

steps/15.description: Cholelithiasis in 2 of 12 patients, both requiring cholecystectomy - at around age 40 and, strikingly, age 15. Expected given deficient mature bile acid synthesis, and worth modelling because juvenile cholelithiasis is an unusual enough finding to be a diagnostic prompt on its own.

evidence.snippet: Two of the patients suffered from adult-onset sensory motor neuropathy.
evidence.explanation: The original clinical description of the adult neuropathy.

steps/16.description: The defining adult phenotype, adult-onset and sensorimotor.

evidence.snippet: she developed a febrile encephalopathy with hemispheric dysfunction, focal convulsive seizures and coma
evidence.explanation: A seizure observed in a named patient, cited in preference to the mouse paper's background summary of the human literature.

evidence.snippet: patients with Amacr deficiency accumulate C27-bile acid intermediates, pristanic and phytanic acid and display sensorimotor neuropathy, seizures and relapsing encephalopathy
evidence.explanation: Corroborates seizures as an established feature. Graded OTHER because the sentence summarises the human literature as background to a mouse study rather than reporting patient data.

steps/17.description: Seizures, including focal convulsive seizures during encephalopathic episodes.

evidence.snippet: One patient also had pigmentary retinopathy, suggesting Refsum disease
evidence.explanation: Documents the retinopathy and the differential it prompted.

evidence.snippet: In 5/9 adult patients, retinitis pigmentosa was detected at a median age of 45 years (range 30-61). The median delay to diagnosis of AMACR deficiency after the diagnosis of retinitis pigmentosa was 24 years (range 0-33).
evidence.explanation: Gives both the frequency in adults and the diagnostic delay, which is what makes this phenotype a practical entry point to the diagnosis.

evidence.snippet: For all three, there were no visual complaints, but retinal multimodal imaging and electroretinography suggested subtle retinal dysfunction
evidence.explanation: Graded PARTIAL because it extends the phenotype rather than confirming it as stated: three siblings had measurable retinal dysfunction with no visual symptoms and no overt pigmentary retinopathy, so the retinal involvement is broader than the frank retinitis pigmentosa this phenotype names.

steps/18.description: Present in one of the two original adult patients, where it suggested Refsum disease - both disorders accumulate phytanic acid, so the retinopathy is a shared consequence rather than a coincidental overlap. The natural-history cohort found it in 5 of 9 adults at a median age of 45, and it is typically the *first* manifestation: the median delay from diagnosing retinitis pigmentosa to diagnosing AMACR deficiency was 24 years, with a range to 33. That number is the single most actionable fact in this entry - an unexplained adult retinitis pigmentosa is a reason to measure pristanic acid.

evidence.snippet: All adult patients subsequently developed neurological signs and symptoms after the age of 40 years; most frequently neuropathy, ataxia and cognitive decline with prior normal cognitive functioning.
evidence.explanation: Names ataxia among the most frequent adult neurological signs.

steps/19.description: Ataxia, among the most frequent neurological signs in the adult natural-history cohort, developing after age 40.

evidence.snippet: most frequently neuropathy, ataxia and cognitive decline with prior normal cognitive functioning
evidence.explanation: Establishes cognitive decline as acquired rather than developmental.

steps/20.description: Cognitive decline in adults with previously normal cognitive function - the "with prior normal cognitive functioning" qualifier matters, because it separates this from the developmental picture and makes it a degenerative feature.

evidence.snippet: All adult patients showed a typical MRI pattern involving the thalami and gray matter structures of the pons and midbrain.
evidence.explanation: Reports the imaging pattern in all adults in the cohort. Note the children in the same cohort showed no brain MRI abnormalities.

steps/21.description: A typical MRI pattern involving the thalami and the gray matter structures of the pons and midbrain, present in every adult patient in the natural-history cohort. Because it is consistent, it is a recognition cue rather than merely a finding - and it explains why these patients are so often worked up for mitochondrial disease first.

evidence.snippet: there is a risk of liver fibrosis/cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma in these patients, requiring active monitoring
evidence.explanation: Establishes HCC as a disease risk with a surveillance implication - and, read against the cholic acid trial, reframes the HCC seen there as disease rather than drug.

steps/22.description: Hepatocellular carcinoma, on a background of liver fibrosis and cirrhosis risk. The cohort authors conclude explicitly that this requires active monitoring, which makes it a surveillance obligation rather than an incidental association.

edges/8.description: Deficient mature C24 bile acid synthesis alters biliary composition, which is the established route to gallstone formation. The intermediate step is known in general bile acid physiology but has not been measured in AMACR deficiency specifically.

evidence.snippet: Pristanic and phytanic acids accumulated in livers of Amacr-/- mice after a phytol diet.
evidence.explanation: Direct demonstration that dietary phytol drives accumulation of these metabolites when AMACR is absent.

edges/21.description: Dietary phytol is the source of the pristanic and phytanic acid that accumulate behind the enzymatic block, so intake sets the size of the accumulating pool.

evidence.snippet: In all three patients we discovered a deficiency of alpha-methylacyl-CoA racemase (AMACR).
evidence.explanation: Original identification of the enzyme deficiency in the index patients.

genes/0.notes: Encodes alpha-methylacyl-CoA racemase. Worth knowing when searching: this symbol is far more prominent in the prostate-cancer literature, where the protein is the P504S immunohistochemical marker, than in the peroxisomal-disease literature. That is a Named Entity Confusion hazard for anyone mining datasets or papers by gene symbol, and none of the evidence in this entry comes from that body of work.

evidence.snippet: Children's transaminase levels normalized during treatment, while adults' levels remained normal throughout.
evidence.explanation: The paediatric biochemical benefit that supports treatment in children.

evidence.snippet: In adults, however, the balance shifts negatively, with side effects outweighing the (biochemical) benefits.
evidence.explanation: Graded PARTIAL because it supports the treatment for one population while explicitly arguing against it in another - the age split is the finding, not a caveat on it.

treatments/0.description: Bile acid replacement suppresses production of the toxic C27 intermediates and supplies the mature bile acid the pathway cannot make. The prospective trial including six AMACR patients gives an unusually clear age-split result: children tolerated it, allowing higher doses, and normalised their transaminases, whereas adults had more side effects - chiefly diarrhoea - and their transaminases had been normal throughout, so the authors concluded the balance shifts negatively in adults. Pristanic acid did not respond in either group.

evidence.snippet: Pristanic acid levels were highly elevated and dietary modification was recommended.
evidence.explanation: The clinical recommendation; note it is a recommendation, not a tested outcome.

treatments/1.description: Recommended on the basis of markedly elevated pristanic acid, and mechanistically supported by the mouse, where phytol intake is the difference between a normal animal and a lethal disease. No trial has tested it in patients, and pristanic acid did not fall on cholic acid, so this is the arm of the disease that bile acid replacement does not reach.

open_questions/0.rationale:
The mouse and the human disagree on whether the genotype alone is sufficient. Amacr-null mice are clinically symptomless on standard chow and need phytol provocation to become ill; patients eating an ordinary diet accumulate pristanic acid and develop neuropathy, hepatic disease or encephalopathy without any special exposure.
The obvious reading is a dose difference - laboratory chow is low in phytol relative to a human diet containing dairy fat and ruminant meat - and if that reading is right, dietary restriction should be able to move patients toward the healthy end of the same curve. That is the reasoning behind recommending dietary modification, and it is currently an inference from the mouse rather than a tested result in patients.
But the alternative readings have not been excluded: mice may handle branched-chain fatty acids through routes humans lack, or the human disease may depend on a lifetime of accumulation that a 36-week mouse experiment cannot represent. The cholic acid trial is a relevant negative here - pristanic acid fluctuated and stayed elevated under a treatment that corrected the bile acid arm, showing that this arm is not incidentally controlled by treating the other one.
This is recorded as HUMAN_MODEL_MISMATCH rather than KNOWLEDGE_GAP because evidence exists in both species and they diverge on the sufficiency of the genotype; the open question is what that divergence means for humans.
